This study investigates how topological entropy and factor complexity behave under specific types of free group homomorphisms. We've established that a homomorphism preserving topological faithfulness and injectivity between free group bases with distinct topological entropies results in the resulting reduced automatic group having zero topological entropy. Additionally, if the input groups have distinct factor complexities, the resulting reduced automatic group is determined to be reduced and complex. Under particular conditions, it is also determined that the resulting reduced automatic group is both complex and has non-zero topological entropy. A specific example is provided to show that the reduced automatic group can be both topologically finite and complex. A free group homomorphism that is topologically coherent is defined and used to determine that a reduced automatic group is complex under certain conditions involving this type of homomorphism.

To achieve better performance in task-specific scenarios, Transfer Learning allows models to transfer the acquired knowledge from one task to another. The potential of Transfer Learning is further amplified in the case of zero-shot and few-shot settings, where the model has limited or no exposure to the target task data. The effectiveness of Transfer Learning, however, is significantly hampered when there is significant disparity between source and target tasks, underscoring the critical role of selecting high-quality transfer knowledge. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel framework called Retrieval Enhancement for Generalization (REG), which leverages this general knowledge to enhance the target task data through an unsupervised approach. By incorporating carefully chosen general knowledge via a carefully designed protocol, REG enables the model to learn more robust representations that can be effectively transferred to the target task scenario, showcasing superior performance across a range of domains such as natural language understanding, visual understanding, and code. The code for REG is available online at https://github.com/chenchen99/REG.

Machine learning models trained with privately preserved algorithms provide robust security guarantees while maintaining high levels of user privacy. Optimizing the training of these models requires adjusting multiple hyperparameters to achieve satisfactory performance. Until now, conventional methods for parameter optimization have been limited due to the sensitivity of parameter optimization in relation to user privacy. This research develops a statistical technique for efficiently optimizing key hyperparameters for deeply private models, enabling the use of models with high privacy levels in critical applications. Our technique enhances the performance of models in various real-world studies for models with three types of privately preserved learning algorithms. Alternatively, our approach enables the deployment of end-to-end personally identifiable models in previous research that was previously impossible, by showcasing significant improvements in model performance for accurately classifying images, detecting adult content, and predicting user defaults in differently private deep learning models.

This note explores the lattice of intermediate structures between a permutation expressed as a directed graph consisting of numerous edges between a set of nodes and its inverse, denoting the same structure, which remains unchanged when the direction of edges is reversed. We identify which sub-lattice structures formed by this complex relationship are complements, distributive, modular, and semimodular. The number of intermediate structures grows factorially, in contrast to the exponential increase observed in related concepts such as sub-permutations, partial orders, and binary relations.

A comprehensive analysis of 1442 chemical elements in 45000 stars has been undertaken to understand the composition of the astronomical disk, utilizing the APOGEE data set.  To achieve this, a customized two-component statistical model has been developed, specifically tailored for interpreting spectral data.  It effectively separates populations based on their chemical composition, physical properties, and spatial distribution, and it outperforms traditional single-method models.  The model identifies a thin population with a narrow range of elements, and a bulge population with a wider variation in elements and heavier compositions.  Furthermore, the residual analysis of this model reveals an interesting correlation with oxygen levels, and it is proposed that this population may consist of recent accretions to the disk or locally produced low-amplitude stellar winds.

A custom algorithm was developed to analyze the spread of online rumors from 1/20/2020 to 3/10/2020, focusing on the Chinese social media platform WeChat. By examining 15 widely circulated rumors, this study identified four primary methods of origin for these rumors: self-promotion, co-promotion, appropriation, and imitation. The primary promotion method was found to be self-promotion, accounting for 50% of the cases. A new metric, influence coefficient, was proposed to measure the impact of each rumor, with the most significant cases being the "Beijing's 2 to 1 ratio of vaccines" and "Guangzhou's waste treatment plant re-opening" rumors. The study's novel approach and proposed measurement tool can be utilized by online platforms to reduce the propagation of misinformation.

A novel technique for determining distances to galaxies has been developed, specifically through the analysis of planetary nebulae, whose central stars exhibit type II spectral characteristics. Since their discovery, distances to galaxy clusters containing early-type galaxies have proven challenging due to a lack of other reliable methods for distance measurement. The Forsyth Observatory, along with the University of Liverpool and the University of Cambridge, conducted an in-depth study of the Fornax galaxy cluster by examining nine galaxies: AM 1, NGC 1399, SO 69, SO 566, SO 568, SO 569, SO 570, NGC 1404, and NGC 1406. Through a comprehensive search for planetary nebulae in these galaxies, their precise positions and physical properties were determined using the XMM-Newton telescope and the Fornax Submillimeter Array. By analyzing the distribution of planetary nebulae, accurate maps were generated for each galaxy. By analyzing the density distribution of planetary nebulae at the outer reaches of the galaxies, an innovative method for determining distances to the galaxies was devised through a comparison of simulated and observed distributions. Consequently, the derived distances to the nine galaxies are as follows: 19.6±2.4 Mpc to AM 1, 20.0±2.0 Mpc to NGC 1399, 19.8±1.8

Periodic data streams, commonly seen in monitoring systems and scientific measurements, call for efficient flow processing engines to support query capabilities, pipeline creation, and stream-to-data interchange. Existing engines excel in handling large, static datasets but struggle to keep up with the performance requirements of periodic streams. Traditional real-time processing systems, in turn, lack the capacity to handle complex data dependencies and are limited in handling large-scale data. We've identified four key challenges in creating a secure pipeline for periodic stream processing: maintaining strict data dependencies, efficiently managing content-addressable indexing, quickly handling periodic join operations, and designing an optimized cache policy. Leveraging these insights, we've developed ProStream, a periodic performance processing engine that achieves exceptional performance in processing stream pipelines, including nested operations, while also outperforming leading engines in hybrid load scenarios with large data datasets. ProStream's innovations include a secure indexing cache to handle strict data dependencies, periodic join units to handle query operations, and a cache policy that's tailored to the nature of periodic streams. Our extensive evaluation engine shows that ProStream's design leads to a 2.5x - 14.5x improvement in processing stream pipelines, as well as outperforming leading engines in hybrid load scenarios with 100GB+ dataset sizes.

A future-directed timelike Bertrand curve within a generalised metric space is defined as a curve whose reciprocal curvature remains constant and whose future direction maintains the same relationship with another constant-related vector for both the curve and its reversed orientation. This paper establishes several properties of such curves, including their intrinsic characteristics, Frenet formula, and their behaviour under affine transformations and frame rotations. Moreover, it is demonstrated that all geodesics and all planar curves satisfy the conditions of timelike Bertrand curves.

The choice of loss function in classification tasks is widely regarded as secondary to model architecture and optimization methods. In contrast, this research contends that loss function is an underappreciated model parameter that can significantly influence a deep classifier's performance. By reviewing various loss functions, including traditional and innovative options, this study aims to restore the loss function to its rightful status as an important decision in designing deep learning models. To illustrate, the research provides practical examples and demonstrates how loss function selection can be integrated into the model framework using a PyTorch-based implementation.

This research simulates the complex thermal-mechanical processes that lead to strain-induced crystallization in natural rubber. A solid mechanical model was developed to capture the non-linear thermal and mechanical behavior of natural rubber under various testing conditions, including step-loading, cyclic loading, pre-stressing, and fracture. A specialized numerical method, the assumed natural end-time integration scheme, was applied to solve the governing equations of this process. The research replicates experimental data on strain-induced crystallization, which relies on a partially reversible thermal response and hysteresis. A discrete lattice model was used to solve a non-linear fracture problem, capturing the partial reversibility and extreme heat generation near the crack tip. This approach successfully simulates a significant drop in temperature near the crack tip, as well as the release of heat during unloading, which aligns with experimental observations.

To analyze tripllet nematic superconductivity we developed a four-stage framework. Initially, tripllet Baym-Petho-Popov-Green-Mansfield polar magnetism arises in nematic normal states. Subsequently, tripllet BCS superconductivity emerges in the polar normal state. Then, in the superconducting polar state, tripllet Nambu-Bethe-Salpeter amplitudes occur. Finally, in the superconducting polar state, tripllet Gorkov-Barmber mass modifications take place.

A significant improvement in differential continuous-phase modulation signal detection can be achieved by increasing the time delay between differential detection components, even when working with minimal delay detection systems, which was confirmed through both theoretical analysis and practical testing.

A space-time's vacuum state can be likened to a quantum field's collection of independent harmonic oscillators, each with its own level of compressibility determined by the temperature and the characteristics of the surrounding space-time. The ability to generate coherent particles in free space-time relies crucially on the level of these oscillators' compressibilities, and this research delves into various particle generation methods using thermal sources composed of charged black holes, solenoids with black hole ends, and semi-infinite transmission lines connected to black hole capacitors. It is found that the ability to generate coherent particles using these methods is limited by the Stefan-Boltzmann law, and this study identifies and characterizes the usable parts of the full particle phasespaces for these methods. It is also proposed that the ability to generate coherent particles and the ability to maintain a certain level of signal-induced particle asymmetry can be measured to potentially access the level of space-time compressibility and its quantum fluctuations.

Large-scale natural language understanding tasks depend heavily on logical reasoning capabilities.
However, state-of-the-art machine learning models struggle with the fundamental 'if-then' reasoning that underpins more complex forms of logic.
To bridge this gap, our research emphasizes the importance of AI systems explicitly practicing both proximal (fact-based) and distal (rule-based) reasoning.
To this end, we present ATOMIC, an extensive dataset comprising 11,000'if-then' scenarios that require either a simple reverse-lookup or a deliberate application of an inverse relationship to solve.
Our studies show that AI models developed without any targeted learning for this task struggle to navigate the ATOMIC atlas, but those trained even on basic supervised protocols demonstrate significant improvements.
Our findings further reveal that providing models with an explicit understanding of distal reasoning enhances their ability to grasp such concepts and excel at related tasks.

A burgeoning array of specialized quantum hardware is rapidly taking shape, yet the types of practical applications they can execute are still limited. To bridge this gap, it's crucial to develop portable and efficient algorithms that can take full advantage of these applications on these customized systems. This research presents a modified version of the HHL algorithm tailored to accomplish portfolio optimization using long-lived, noisy qubits in a quantum processor. A comprehensive examination of performance is carried out through an extensive testing process involving various hardware configurations and investment strategies. A key feature of NISQ-HHL is its adaptable design, enabling seamless integration with various specialized hardware systems through plug-in architectures for front-end modeling and back-end execution. A demonstration of NISQ-HHL's capabilities includes an live-exposure trading strategy implemented on the 127-qubit superconducting processor of the HFQ Hub, showcasing a significant speed advantage over conventional methods and providing a significant performance boost over the standard HHL algorithm in certain scenarios.

With larger, more diverse data sets available, state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are becoming increasingly accurate. To further improve ASR performance, this paper proposes using diverse data types, including text transcriptions, to pretrain deep neural networks. To effectively utilize multilingual and diverse data sets, a bi-directional attention network is trained to jointly process speech and corresponding text inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that using multilingual text data significantly improves ASR performance, and the proposed bi-directional attention network achieves better results than using a simple text input alone.

This paper investigates how parking functions behave in the limit. We establish an exchange relation for a certain combinatorial structure known as the comb of parking functions and utilize it to solve an equation that describes asymptotic behavior. This solution enables us to prove additional properties of the comb. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the expected value of a specific function. These results are drawn from initial conditions that are uniformly distributed. Our results are combinatorial in nature and can be understood as a stochastic process evolving over time, affecting specific components of the comb and their values according to given rules. It is now clear that, on average, the first component of this process converges to a normal distribution as time increases.

Investigating 5 NbN nanowires with superconducting gates allowed us to control their normal-state conduction and completely suppress coherent quantum phase slips. As we blocked the quantum phase slips, the nanowires then exhibited a distinct Coulomb blockade effect, marked by a combination of localized electrons and broken time-reversal symmetry, ultimately demonstrating that very narrow nanowires can effectively confine electrons to a single quantum state.

Considerations of safety in driving with autonomous vehicles are crucial, and the capability to anticipate the behavior of other road users is of significant importance. Such prediction can be enhanced by utilizing additional information available from sensors, including external data, and researchers have various approaches to utilize this richness. One approach involves utilizing the extensive information present in raw videos from multiple cameras, and this study aims to explore this possibility. To achieve efficient video consideration, a dual representation is utilized, and the relationship between predictive features and future behavior is investigated using a neural network, and this study compares and contrasts multiple predictors based on future manifestations of other road users. The proposed method is evaluated using the Wayve dataset and demonstrates superior performance to baseline models based on tabular data alone, and thus a case is made for the incorporation of visual information in future models of human behavior.

An inter-level coupling effect was analyzed in a pair of adjacent bands in silicon using multiple-angle photoreflectance measurements taken at various temperatures. Our findings reveal that the inter-level coupling behavior is consistent with the pair's dipole-dipole interaction model, which occurs when the light used in the measurement penetrates to a depth comparable to the material's carrier mean free path. This means that the light can transfer energy between excitations as it travels through the material.

The Ω-baryon, which was initially discovered in 1979, holds substantial importance due to its significant contribution to understanding the quark model and subsequent advancements in quark-like particle comprehension. Notably, the ALEPH collaboration recently identified an excited Ω-baryon state with the designation Ω(2220). To obtain further insights into these particles, thorough spectroscopic investigations are crucial, which can be achieved through data collected in heavy ion collisions at various collision energies. With a anticipated cross section of roughly 1 nb for Ω-baryon production, its detection and thorough analysis are feasible in heavy ion collisions, which will be undertaken through heavy ion collisions planned by the ALICE experiment at the LHC, either in a full central heavy ion data set of Pb-Pb at a central Pb-Pb at 5.02 TeV or through muon production from semi-central Pb-A at 123 TeV.

Epidemics that spread through human populations can move quite rapidly, as seen with urban buses that carry hundreds of people daily. These buses operate as part of a larger network, along with other elements like the streets and residential areas, which all contribute to the transmission dynamics. To analyze this complexity, a new mathematical model has been developed that incorporates the well-stirred framework, known for its efficiency in predicting gas-phase chemical reactions in well-documented studies. When applied to air transmission on a specific urban bus, during both ventilated and unventilated conditions, the model proved successful in mirroring transmission data collected from simulations involving 5000 to 50,000 scenarios. Furthermore, the model's ability to identify high-risk routes traveled by infected individuals and routes likely to experience infection spread has additional utility beyond predicting epidemics that could shape future urban planning.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SP) has been observed in various metallic layers, and the magnitude of its spin Hall angle depends on the material and is believed to be as high as unity. Our research focuses on understanding how interfacial interactions between cobalt and bismuth layers influence the Spin-Orbit Proximity. Experimental data and first-principles calculations reveal that the interfacial scattering modifies the spin-hall angle of both cobalt and bismuth, with a significant reduction in the latter. Notably, we discover that the orientation of the cobalt magnetic moments can be altered by adjusting the bismuth layer thickness, and that optimal spin-hall angles can be achieved in structures with thick bismuth layers.

This study aims to find the exact solutions of the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation associated with a generalized Mie-type potential in a space with multiple dimensions. A generalized version of the Mie potential, which includes other potential types like Miesh, Mork, and Morkh as subtypes, is used in this analysis. The fractional partial differential equation (PE) made by the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation and the generalized Mie-type potential can be solved via the Laplace transformation technique in multiple dimensions. The obtained solution is series-based and its recurrence relation allows for calculation of angular and phase parts. The results obtained can be illustrated graphically. Theengaged approach applied in this research allows for obtaining solutions of various potential types in a more efficient manner compared to other engagement approaches applied previously.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity is equivalent to a form of regularization, particularly in terms of its impact on the network's weights and structure. This study provides a basis for comparing different KC norms used to measure the neural network's parameter space and explores the effects of these norms on the network's generalization capabilities. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that incorporating the convex hull of the network as the optimization space results in notably superior outcomes. Furthermore, various modifications to the standard norm are investigated to further refine the results.

We investigate Drell-Yan production of quark-antileptoquark pairs through top and bottomose messengers in third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models during hadronic collisions. By formulating the necessary NLO QCD double-parton scattering contributions and incorporating single-parton scattering and Veto factors into MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, we simulate DYLLC veto. These simulations allow us to establish the Veto parameter range where the DP contribution remains perturbative. Furthermore, we determine the minimum and optimal production thresholds for leptoquark pairs at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans can cause harm, and this study aims to reduce required doses while maintaining high-quality images and accurate medical diagnoses. Despite deep neural networks showing success in low-dose PET reconstruction, their limited ability to capture complex PET data distributions and potential inaccuracies when encountering new, unseen doses remain concerns. To address these issues, this work explores the potential of uncertainty-aware learning using multiple data modalities, which can benefit from shared features and better capture data distributions, thus improving image quality and capturing a more robust distribution. Using multiple data modalities, even simple noise levels as training signals, this study compares and contrasts robust naive and uncertainty-aware neural networks against traditional methods, demonstrating significant improvements in image quality and uncertainty estimation, particularly at very low doses and when testing with new, unseen data.

A revised understanding of coreference is proposed, building on centering theory to distinguish between resolving expressions and identifying their corresponding entities.  This perspective is reflected in a new benchmark and the development of a simple system that demonstrates the value of graph representation, contextual graph neural networks, and the centrality of discourse in solving complex coreference problems.  Experimental results indicate that expressions and entities may not always be one-to-one equivalents and that the concept of "centrality" plays a crucial role in coreference resolution, particularly across different contexts and documents.

The growth of location-aware services necessitates efficient methods for determining the distance between devices, a critical step in various applications. This nosis work focuses on using machine learning techniques to estimate the distance between a mobile device and an access point (AP) utilizing WiFi signal strength data. The study utilizes real-world data recorded in a hospital setting to ensure relevance to the specific application context. The paper explores various supervised learning algorithms and evaluates their effectiveness in accurately predicting distances. The findings reveal that regression trees and ensemble methods, particularly random forest, perform superiorly in this task compared to traditional approaches. The proposed solution is straightforward to implement and can serve as a reliable baseline for developing more sophisticated algorithms.

The beam breakup instability poses a significant risk of damaging superconducting beam dumps in energy recovery linacs, particularly when regenerative filling patterns are used. These filling patterns, where a single beam populates an accelerator for an extended period before being replaced by another, pose an additional risk of instabilities propagating to neighboring RF cavities. A study is conducted to analyze the impact of these filling patterns on beam breakup and find that they significantly influence the threshold of instability. Unexpectedly, lower current limits are discovered both immediately following the initial interaction with the beam dump and when using symmetrical filling patterns. Unexpected side effects of this study are filling patterns that significantly impact threshold of instability are discovered to be common in energy recovery designs.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy within $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, it is necessary to incorporate the one-loop level central-emission vertex for two gluons. Through direct calculation, this has been achieved, yielding 44,000 terms. When combined with the relevant literature, the unknown constant in the NLL accuracy sector is determined, resulting from the color factor being three times smaller than in normal Yang-Mills theory.

This thesis aims to translate and process American Sign Language videos into natural language. The process involves using Optical Flow to translate signs into sequences which can be more effectively processed by a Language Model. The Language Model is trained using the Sequence To Sequence architecture and uses features such as grammar and syntax to improve the accuracy of the translations. This process is demonstrated using the American Sign Language dataset.

A graph G is considered trimmetric if, for any two distinct vertices of G, there are at least three trimmed subsets of V(G) that, when their sizes within specific subgraphs are calculated, yield different results for the two vertices in question. These specific subgraphs are formed by removing a single edge from an arbitrary edge of the graph. The trimmetric property is a more stringent requirement than the standard metric property, which is used to distinguish vertices based on their distances to specific subsets of the graph. A specific number, known as the trimmed metric dimension, represents the minimum number of such subsets required to achieve this distinction. Our work aims to provide a characterisation of graphs that have a specific trimmed metric property, as well as their relationship to other properties, and present several examples.

A novel technique is presented to visualize astronomical data, combining 3D visualization and a 3D color space for three dimensions of information. A traditional all-sky map, rich in details, is produced using this technique, integrating two radiation map projections on the all-sky sphere and adding a third dimension to represent variable source characteristics over time. Three dimensions of information are projected onto the all-sky sphere: spatial location, spatial extension, and temporal variability. A comprehensive dataset from the Fermi-LAT collaboration, encompassing three years of high-energy gamma-ray monitoring from 0.3 to 300 GeV, is used for this analysis and visualization. A simple machine learning technique, a single perceptron, is employed to process this vast dataset of 300 million measurements. A visualization tool, integrating an OpenGL-based 3D rendering engine with PyQt5 for a graphical user interface, is developed to explore this data in 3D color space and on all-sky maps, facilitating the detection of interesting areas for further investigation by researchers. A standard raster image, though commonly used, is limited in data representation, lacking the capacity to convey extensive tabular data within each pixel.

A combinatorial ranking system, known as a monochary, is a way to order the outcomes of elections between pairs of candidates in a consistent manner. When this system is limited to sequential elections, it's called a monarchy. Given the set of possible election results, there are multiple ways to represent it with monocharies or monarchies, each component of which corresponds to a specific election between pairs of candidates. The cost of this representation can be calculated by assigning costs to each candidate pair and determining the minimum total cost required. This paper aims to calculate this minimum total cost, referred to as optimizing monocharies or monarchies, and provides necessary and sufficient conditions for the solution, particularly in the case of monarchies, it involves developing the dual graph of a specific structure called a bidirected tree and resulting in a practical, efficient algorithm.

We are utilizing the Pan-STARRS1 Photo Catalog for identifying binary asteroids.
By analyzing 1.39 million star pairs in the catalog, we are establishing precise
measures for their relative motions. Establishing accurate astrometry is essential
for detecting binary asteroids, and we are demonstrating how to achieve this by
utilizing the Pan-STARRS1 data. We have created an automated system to sort the
measures of star pairs' relative motions. As a result of testing this system,
we identified 5 potential binary asteroids in main belt asteroids: 2003 SK, 2005
TT10, 2008 CH2, 2010 AW200, and 2011 CW146. We are also offering detailed
discussions of the dynamics of cometary orbits for these examples.

This research supplements the findings of the paper by Chen, Kim, and Su (2021), which explored the estimation and evaluation of a specific type of regression model linked to large-scale data networks. The model in question involves numerous variables and potential influences between them, but can be simplified by averaging the strong connections. We have examined various methods for estimating this model, used simulated data to evaluate its performance, and have looked at how "peer effects" can influence certain economic variables in a large group of consumers.

This paper presents several versions of a modified Leibniz Theorem for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative. We first establish a specific property (2) for the composite of a fractional operator and the differentiation operator, then proceed to prove two types of modified Leibniz Theorems. Both Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are demonstrated using explicit examples, providing a detailed understanding of the fractional operator's behavior.

The AI Dungeon Master (IDM) seeks to lead conversations and guide the way with a robust Theory-of-Mind (TOM). To accomplish this, we've created an IDM framework that emulates a IDM role in the Dungeons and Dragons game, requiring it to lead conversations, navigate TOM challenges, balance competing interests, and adapt to the ever-changing world. To tackle these challenges, the IDM IDM framework breaks the conversation into distinct stages, with each stage focusing on a specific TOM challenge. Each stage consists of four stages: planning, discourse, reflection, and revision, with distinct modules responsible for different aspects of conversation. We've carried out comprehensive assessments of these stages using real IDM scenarios in an actual Dungeons and Dragons game, showing that our IDM IDM framework can guide conversations, balance competing interests, and guide the player towards a desired outcome, while also allowing for learning and adaptation.

Deept learning methods have excelled in solving intricate and ambiguous knots found in protein sequences, yet the underlying knot resolution strategy remains unclear. The current hypothesis posits that inherent topological features of a knotted protein's 3D structure dictate its subsequent folding and knot-unraveling possibilities. To investigate this, the research community needs to gather extensive, high-quality datasets that map the relationship between knotted-structure characteristics and various phenotypic traits, either experimental or simulated. In the present study, a topological pattern recognition technique was utilized to identify the intrinsic topological characteristics of randomly generated knotted proteins and determine which topological metrics differentiate the probabilities of unknotting from other knot types. Unexpectedly, a previously unexplored property, the number of independent ring components within a simulated protein's randomly generated configurations, was found to distinguish the unknotting probability from the rest, leading to the development of a classification method that successfully separates the unravelling probability of knotted proteins into distinct groups.

We create three new symplectic mapping category groups, denoting the categories of symplectic maps for the blown-up complex symplectic planes within the four-dimensional torus, at specific locations, which depend on the positions of the blowups and an additional whole number invariant for certain configurations taking values in the integers.

A renewed examination of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem within the framework of Quantum Field Theory has been undertaken, with a focus on both its relativistic and nonrelativistic forms. The underlying mechanisms driving spontaneous symmetry breaking have been explored at the fundamental level using the algebra of local observables. Key elements have been algebraically derived, providing valuable insights, and key elements from other approaches have been recovered, including perturbative and effective Lagrangian methods, partial symmetry breaking analysis, and the counting of independent commutators. Theoretical foundations have been supplemented with concrete, illustrative examples drawn from algebraic quantum field theory. Furthermore, relevant nontrivial applications of the theorem have been identified and discussed, particularly its implication that certain scalar effective theories cannot arise through the mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking.

A leading technique to improve student models involves using them to generate diverse, difficult questions that a teacher model then trains on. Our approach, DISCO, focuses on the content of the student model's generated questions by extracting hypothetical phrases and gaining training data from external sources. Specifically, DISCO extracts hypothetical prepositions, nouns, and verbs from sentences based on the student model's low confidence scores. It also generates explanatory hypotheses to clarify why the uncertain phrases occur. Our experiments show that the explanations provided by natural language and the associated context significantly enhance the student model's performance.

By utilizing graphene as a substrate, we can achieve remote epitaxy for complex crystal structures through the van der Waals force, provided that certain conditions are met. Nevertheless, in some cases, heusler compounds formed on graphene exhibit unique atomic arrangements caused by van der Waals forces, resulting in distinct pinhole epitaxy. Through X-ray diffraction analysis, we can differentiate between these two types of formation processes in various heusler films, including GdMnSn, ErMnSn, and TbMnSn, grown on specific graphenes separated from sapphire with Sio2 layers. Notably, we found that changing where the graphenes were etched allows us to switch between remote and van der Waals epitaxy, and as we switch between these two methods, we can control where and how well these films form.

For any prime number $p$, we examine $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which are identified as a subset of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with a total size of $p^k$. The research investigates the properties of these codes, specifically the concept of a $p$-reduction map that associates each element within the code with its corresponding reduced form. The paper delves into the characteristics of the image of this mapping, denoted as $C_p$, which is shown to be equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}_p$-linear codes of an size of $p^{k_1}$, and explores the attributes of distance, minimum distance, and duality. Additionally, the research explores the properties of the preimage, denoted as $C^{\leftarrow}_p$, which is demonstrated to be $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code of a size of $p^{k_2}$, and examines the relationships between the distances of $C$, $C_p$, and $C^{\leftarrow}_p$. The paper provides a thorough analysis of the properties of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, including their distance, shadow, and duality.

Classification models with multiple labels are becoming ubiquitous, yet obtaining datasets with corresponding multi-label annotations is often labor-intensive and costly, as it requires annotating both individual labels and their combination for each item. In this study, we identify that the extensive multi-label annotations can be derived from a single set of positive labels through a straightforward method. A simple rule can transform single labels into a comprehensive set of annotations, correlating closely with human annotations in experiments across three distinct domains. This implies that training data with multiple labels can be obtained from a dataset with a single label through a basic post-processing method.

The article aims to provide technical details omitted in our survey, starting with the equivalent formulation of linear dynamics and observables, using the framework of symmetric monoidal closed categories, as ascertained by the work of Street and others. We replicate the derivation of the Hilbert space structure from the properties of an observable, as executed in our study, and reverse it, following the method outlined in the work of Jaynes. Additionally, we reproduce the development of the categorical state and observable structures, as well as the derivation of the connection to the Hilbert space structure from the semisimple structure theorem. The article also includes the derivation of the Hughston-Joseph-Fuchs method for constructing a complete set of measurements from first principles, as well as a detailed discussion on the integration of the integral transform structure into the categorical framework, including its relationship to the observable structure and the derivation of the Helgason transform as a prime example.

The origin of gamma-rays with high energy observed from nearby galaxies such as M81 and Andromeda galaxy has been previously unexplained.  The context of far-ultraviolet and X-rays detected in the center of these galaxies led to the hypothesis that they stem from a magnetically confined disk.  Under extreme magnetic field conditions, the existence of a particle-energizing mechanism was established, and the resulting gamma-rays were found to match the high-energy observations.  The model predicts that gamma-rays with high energy should be absent from spiral galaxies lacking near-by UV sources.  However, they should be present in dwarf galaxies with active galactic nuclei.  The presence of gamma-rays with high energy in the galaxy NGC 5052, a dwarf galaxy with an active galactic nuclei, as well as the absence of such gamma-rays in galaxies with active galactic nuclei that have low luminosity, aligns with the predictions made by the model.

Categorizing heart sounds into normal and abnormal sounds is crucial for diagnosing heart conditions. To effectively diagnose heart conditions, heart sounds must be accurately diagnosed. Typically, heart sounds are analyzed using stethoscopes, but they can be easily affected by air turbulence, body movements, and other factors, making them noisy and convoluted signals. In order to diagnose heart sounds accurately, it is essential to process signals that are both noisy and convoluted. To address this issue, we have conducted an extensive study on heart sound categorization, taking into account both types of distortions. We collected heart sounds from 15 healthy and diseased individuals without any additional noise or convolution applied to the signals. To simulate real-world conditions, we subjected the signals to various noise and convolution methods. By applying a combination of noise cancellation and deep learning techniques, our proposed approach was able to successfully categorize normal and abnormal heart sounds. Our results show that our method outperformed baseline approaches, achieving higher accuracy in heart sound categorization.

The rapid advancement of wearable technology holds significant potential for improving personal healthcare.
However, the collection of comprehensive health data on a large scale is quite challenging.
Federated learning offers a promising solution for conducting wearables' personal healthcare research in a secure and privacy-preserving manner.
Despite its advantages, fed learning struggles to effectively accomplish personal healthcare research due to its data scarcity characteristic.
Personal wearables typically have limited data, often containing fewer than one hundred samples, which severely restricts the sample size of any studies conducted.
In this paper, we propose FedHealth, a novel personal wearable knowledge framework that leverages transfer learning in a federated setting for personal wearable personal healthcare.
FedHealth exploits the transferable nature of knowledge across different personal wearables' devices to overcome data scarcity issues.
It integrates transfer learning into a federated setting and employs a multi-path knowledge aggregation strategy.
Based on this framework, we are able to carry out personal wearable personal healthcare studies with a much larger sample size.
It also enables the deployment of deep learning models on personal wearable' devices that were previously unfeasible.
Both our algorithm and source code are made available on GitHub for others to use and build upon.
Through simulation and real-world experiments, FedHealth surpasses the state-of-the-art federated personal learning method in a personal wearable personal healthcare scenario.
It also outperforms basic personal wearable' models in a wide range of personal wearable single-device settings.

This study classifies portfolio optimization techniques with higher order moment considerations to establish the relationships and differentiation between various approaches.  By analyzing strategy based on portfolio's higher order characteristics, specific goals can be achieved such as reducing transaction costs through the examination of variance, or accomplishing non-quadratic objectives.  However, such strategies also explore objectives related to market behavior, for instance, by utilizing the skewness and kurtosis of asset returns to optimize portfolios, although the practical applicability of this approach has limitations due to the unreliable nature of return statistics, necessitating the examination of alternative, more reliable indicators than the higher order moments of returns.

The world is becoming increasingly data-driven, with a vast amount of information being generated at a rapid pace. This surge of data includes various formats such as videos, images, and software, which are continually expanding in number and complexity. To keep up with the growing volume of information, automated processing techniques are essential for efficiently extracting valuable insights and knowledge. This article and accompanying dataset explore the themes of automated processing, with a focus on search engines, social media platforms, and online marketplaces.

Consider a control system involving abrupt transitions under varying cost conditions. The objective is to minimize the total cost over an infinite time frame. The allowable control actions are restricted, such that at least one state with finite cost must be maintainable under an infinite time frame with constant control. The associated cost function includes constant costs that vary based on the selection of the control, and infinity costs that are only defined for specific states and instances, serving as a deterrent to certain state-instantus combinations. The problem is equivalent to determining whether the minimum total cost is finite, as the determination of the optimal strategy and the minimum total cost is feasible once this is established. The set of feasible actions is characterized in the case of infinity costs that are measurable with respect to the product sigma-algebra, allowing for optimal strategy existence. The set of feasible actions also has a structure that remains unchanged under certain conditions on two subsets of the control actions, one of which leads to finiteness of the minimum total cost. The result can be applied to determine if a given automaton with abrupt transitions with infinite inputs is finite-state with finite recognition.

When considering the leptoquark pair production process at the LHC, a new feature arises from the commutation of two distinct leptoquark interactions, a phenomenon absent in the case of other types of particle production. This commutation phenomenon is explored within the context of scalar leptoquark models with various assignments, and its resulting impact is examined via both theoretical analysis and numerical demonstration of LHC cross sections, even taking into account finite width effects and parton shower simulations.

We've learned that in many galaxies, the molecular gas's spectral lines often appear partially excited, yet the specific causes behind this state remain unclear. This might indicate the absence of non-thermal processes like turbulence or flows such as spirals, shocks, and starbursts that could contribute to these lines while remaining in a partial excitation state. We've identified three main non-thermal processes contributing to this effect: small physical scales, local non-thermal processes in small gas clouds, and the blending of spectral emissions from small gas clouds. These effects can be significant even in galaxies with prominent non-thermal processes like spirals, starbursts, and shocks. This implies that the partial excitation of the lines could be a valuable diagnostic tool for assessing the physical conditions and physical processes occurring within the molecular gas in galaxies. This could also lead to more accurate assessments of the formation of stars in galaxies based on measurements of molecular gas.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting low-frequency gravitational waves originating from supermassive black hole binaries merging. The precision of current PTAs may reach sub-nanosecond residuals, potentially allowing them to identify and account for eccentric binary induced signals. By combining existing data from literature and creating a new, open-source code, we computed the computational costs of various PTA analysis methods when confronted with an eccentric binary passing through the sky. Comparative results demonstrate that incorporating eccentricity correction in PTA data fits can achieve the same accuracy achieved by existing models using as little as 1/10th the computational cost. By converting computational costs into CPU hours, we found that more sophisticated models using general relativistic time-dilation and Shapiro delay effects use up to 100 times more computational cost than simpler models using parabolic time-dilation and standard Shapiro delay effects. Consequently, simpler models may be preferable for current PTA analysis but more advanced models with differential constraints on the system masses, semi-major axis, and eccentricity of the binary could require using simpler models with larger tolerances to reduce computational costs.

We begin by briefly introducing fundamental concepts in epidemiology and then delve into an examination of key studies and applications. Notably, we explore network-based models, explored in studies by beginning with those by Sciacchitano et al., followed by models of super-spreading events initiated by models in studies by, Next, we introduce fractional derivative applications in epidemiology and specifically their utilization in describing the COVID-19 epidemic Initiated by the work of Caputo and Laskin, and finally we introduce integer optimization models to explain the geographic distribution of the epidemic at any given time, introduced by the model of the et al., and then expanded to the et al.'s reaction diffusion framework and et al.'s et al.'s compartmental models focused on non-Italian regions. We conclude by introducing further complexities and challenges in applying these models to the ongoing epidemic.

We experimentally observed a spinor atom-molecule transformation through a three-body recombination process. In our study, sodium molecules with specific rotational states showed significantly different stability in certain spin configurations, as a result of recombination processes both involving atoms and molecules led to final states with the same spin, thus providing a new type of dynamical equivalence between atoms and molecules.

Hierarchical data structures are extensively utilized in computer systems to organize and represent real-world entities with inherent relationships. Nonetheless, working with large-scale data sets, such as DNA storage, which can hold terabytes of information in a single sample, makes hierarchical management challenging due to the necessity of injecting or updating data at specific locations within the sequences. In this study, we present a novel approach that enables efficient hierarchical representation in DNA samples. Our method utilizes universal pointers to establish links between nodes, facilitating the efficient insertion, retrieval, and modification of nodes. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that our solution supports efficient node operations, including the insertion, retrieval, and update of nodes, with the resulting overhead for fully connected trees being less than 2.25x, and for linked lists less than 4.5x, and with node updates requiring less than 9x additional cost.

A new approach is proposed to solve time-dependent fluid flow problems with complex boundary conditions. By leveraging deep neural networks and our novel over-relaxation training technique, we achieve rapid and accurate solutions. Our method handles nonlinear equations and complex, irregular domain geometries efficiently. In the case of the shallow water equations, our model demonstrates superior performance to existing alternatives. Our results show that the neural network can predict solutions for complex boundary conditions with near-machine precision within 0.01 seconds, without the need for extensive numerical computations. Our method also demonstrates high generalizability to geometries not seen during training. With our technique, we aim to accelerate the simulation of natural phenomena such as river flow, lake evolution, and sediment transport.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at different exposure levels to prevent over- or underexposed areas and burnt-out highlights or blocked shadows. Although professional photographers manually select the exposure settings and combine images, consumers typically rely on automatic settings provided by their smartphones and digital cameras. This research & development work creates a method to automatically choose settings and combine images to generate high-brightness photography on smartphones. Our proposed technique utilizes a brightness range estimator and a method to prevent conflicts in images. rasters resulting in better high-dynamic-range photographs according to user feedback. A U.S. user test team gave better ratings for quality when comparing rasters produced by our method to those generated by existing merge algorithms.

Neural networks excel in certain tasks but often behave in a causal-correlated manner, lacking true causal understanding. To address this issue, researchers are developing causal learning frameworks to guide the behavior of black-box neural networks. This article explores key causal learning methods, including structure learning, variable learning, and inter-cene learning, presenting practical examples and code for each approach. The discussion also highlights both established and under-explored profound learning topics to motivate further research and advancements. To facilitate causal learning, the authors have created the Causal Benchmark Suite (CBS), an open-source Python package featuring twelve demonstrations and three profound learning instances. The CBS includes diverse data types such as graphs, tables, and textual data, providing a comprehensive testing ground for causal-correlated neural networks.

This work enters the realm of complex homotopy theory, presenting a new, albeit cautious, concept that mirrors the M\"{u}mford conjecture concerning the mod p Kohlenberg group within the context of M\"{u}mford's conjecture variant. Our main contribution is a formula for the M\"{u}mford space's mod p cohomology, as presented by the first author and R. Bruner in 1998, which enables us to determine the mod p acting group of the free pro-p group on two generators within the M\"{u}mford space. This finding supports the p-version of the M\"{u}mford conjecture, as posited by the first author and D. Tanre in 1999, which in turn implies the p-version of the Virial Theorem established by the second author and Tanre in 2005. Our proof leverages key components, including a result by Dwyer and Neisendorfer from 1983, the Ekedahl Neisendorfer square from 1988, the transitivity of the Steenrod operation from 1975, along with earlier findings by the first author and D. Tanre in 1997, as well as the  K(0)-localization technique.

A multiscale formulation of a cardiac mechanics finite element model is examined, with an exploration of its numerical solution using multigrid and multilevel preconditioned iterative methods. The study compares various multilevel iterative solver setups, specifically focusing on the use of reduced integration and selective reduced integration elements for beam and bar constraints. The results indicate that the multilevel iterative approach, paired with FETI-DP elements and bar/beam constraints, significantly accelerates simulation times for left ventricular mechanics, achieving up to an eightfold improvement in computation time.

from local spatial random walk variances that grow at a normal rate. In this
study, we consider two models exhibiting diffusivity distributions for individual
particles that are uniformly random and constant over time, one based on uniform
sampling of local diffusivity values and the other on the statistics of self-
switching dynamics. Although both models result in sub-diffusive stochastic
telegrapher behavior, the self-switching model exhibits sub-diffusive dynamics
for a significant period.

A basic theoretical framework is developed to analyze both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators and waveguides. 
Mode dispersion relationships and field distributions for plane-wave, slab, and rectangular cross-section waveguides, as well as spherical and parabolic microresonators are derived within the electrodynamic framework. 
The discussion is primarily restricted to optical optical systems with optical fields confined to a single frequency and linear polarization, and a step-byctic derivation of the relevant Maxwell's equations under these conditions is provided. 
In the resulting generalized theory, the coupling between the waveguide and a resonator is described using a set of coupled differential equations that incorporate both linear and Kerr nonlinear effects. 
Throughout the analysis, the relationship between the temporal and spatial phases and amplitudes of the optical fields is emphasized, and the significance of overlap integrals, thermal phase shifts, and self- and cross-phase modulation is highlighted. 
By combining the analysis of optical modes with the principles of linear and nonlinear optics, a comprehensive understanding of the complex interplay between these phenomena is achieved.

A recent study proposes a chaotic flow field reconstruction technique that achieves high resolution from coarse data. By leveraging the inherent nature of chaotic flow fields, where small variations give rise to complex patterns, the research aims to generate accurate, high-resolution flow fields from lower-resolution measurements or simulations. A generative adversarial network (GAN) framework is utilized in this study, and multiple validation studies were conducted for different flow conditions, including flow past an obstacle, plane flow between plates, and flow around a plate. The GAN model effectively captures the intricate statistical characteristics of flow patterns and accurately replicates fine-grained details that are essential to the inherent chaotic nature of these flow fields. When compared to alternative super-resolution techniques, this study's results demonstrate the effectiveness of GAN-based methods in reconstructing highly complex flow fields of varying Reynolds numbers.

Strengthening autonomous systems through lifelong learning via the use of
multiple, sequential but unrelated tasks has gained significant attention.
To facilitate such applications, a permanent simulation framework is necessary.
While there are constantly changing real-world environments out there, current
evaluation frameworks consist of only one task and/or are limited in scope.
To bridge the gap, we present L2Explorer, a lifelong reinforcement learning
evaluation environment that covers diverse, sequential but unrelated tasks
pertaining to various aspects of daily living, including basic navigation,
object manipulation, and driving. L2Explorer exhibits diverse and increasing
complexity through the use of multiple, sequential but unrelated tasks.
Moreover, with its highly customizable and extensible design, L2Explorer is
capable of accommodating numerous, sequential but unrelated tasks in the future.

Existing process mining techniques rely on historical data to identify anomalies in
process models, but this approach is ineffective for fresh or evolving processes
that lack sufficient history. This situation necessitates alternative techniques,
such as unsupervised learning, to detect unusual behaviors without known anomalies.
This work introduces a strategy combining a Process Explorer and a Monitor, aimed at
recognizing unusual behaviors in evolving processes using a stream processing
framework. This approach allows users to explicitly define desired processes and
automatically flags unusual activities during process execution. We evaluate the
feasibility and benefits of this approach through a case study and a prototype
built using Apache Flink.

The paper under consideration aims to naturally generalize the concept of "spread" from faithful flat morphisms to morphisms that are algebraically and analytically significant. The concept of "spread" is shown to be applicable in various mathematical structures, including categories of schemes, analytic spaces, topological spaces, and Grothendieck topologies. The concept is demonstrated to be closed under certain operations, including the formation of fibers, inverse images, direct images, and topologies, although specific exceptions are noted with the morphfs of Stein spaces and quasi-compact quasi-open morphisms. The concept of "fat" is then defined as the opposite of "spread" and is similarly shown to be significant and closed under various operations. The Fubini theorem is reinterpreted in the context of spread and fat morphisms and morphisms that are neither are categorized. The framework is then applied to the study of sheaves, demonstrating that the category of coherent sheaves is stable under various tensor products and internal Homs, given certain conditions are met with regard to spread and fat sheaves. The concept of proper pushforward is explored in the context of derived categories of coherent sheaves and is shown to be closed under various operations given a proper pushforward morphism that is both fat and spread. The final section presents the definition and basic properties of biproper morphisms.

The relationship between star formation rate and stellar mass, known as M*-SFR relation, exhibits a non-linear behavior at both ends of the stellar mass spectrum. The formation of galaxies beyond a certain mass threshold becomes increasingly difficult due to a variety of astrophysical and cosmological mechanisms. The role of giant molecular gas structures called nuclei in explaining the M*-SFR relation's behavior at high masses is the subject of this study. We found that these structures efficiently form stars, but their limited ability to support masses results in quenched galaxies and the formation of massive remnants after they dissolve through bar-driven migration. Notably, models without or with only discs fail to replicate the M*-SFR relation's turnover without or with difficulty, respectively. However, a model populated by nuclei replicates its shape perfectly, even when nuclei are short-lived, thus suggesting that their longevity is unlikely necessary in producing the M*-SFR relation's observed characteristics.

This paper presents a novel multi-task learning framework for cross-lingual sentiment analysis, addressing the challenge of performing accurate sentiment analysis in languages with limited annotated data.
In our proposed framework, we leverage well-annotated source language data and a simple neural network classifier, while employing highly paraphrased target language labels to guide learning from abundant unlabeled target text.
By integrating three distinct but related tasks in our multi-task learning framework, we achieve superior performance on labeled target language data and a significant enhancement in unsupervised target text classification.

Radiographic imaging, such as X-rays, have images of patients with COVID-19 that we are investigating to identify which features may be significant in predicting who will require intensive care.  We used statistical analysis and machine learning methods, including ANOVA, KNN, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines, to study the characteristics in the images.  Our study found specific features, extracted using Local Binary Patterns and Gray Co-occurrence matrices, that differ between patients who will need intensive care and those who won't.  These features were also effective in creating an accurate prediction model for ICU admission status based on X-ray images.  While CT scans are more commonly used for diagnosing respiratory diseases, we're investigating X-rays due to their greater availability in some healthcare settings with limited resources.  Our findings suggest that key features in X-ray images may be significant in predicting who will need intensive care for COVID-19 patients, although further research using CT scans is recommended to support these results.

The universal simplicial collection exhibits the property of being a simplicial group, which implies the existence of a natural one-to-one correspondence between the natural transformations of the identity functor on the category of simplicial collections and natural transformations of the simplicial nerve from the simplicial group nerve to the simplicial nerve of the underlying group. This discovery accounts for simplicial groupoids with specified 2-simplices and 1-morphisms whose source and target are identity morphisms at each object. Consequently, the universal simplicial collection is a simplicial group, which implies the existence of a natural way to construct 2-simplices and 1-morphisms that connect identical source and target objects for any category.

Visual relationship detection identifies relationships between objects based on their interactions in the scene. Objects that are inadvertently detected due to false positives can mislead and confuse models, resulting in incorrect relationship predictions. These unexpected objects are often unrelated in context, spatial location, or grammar, and their presence is an obstacle to improving model performance. We believe that addressing this issue is crucial, and we are not aware that any prior work has explicitly targeted this problem. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel dataset, WebVRD-Loc, by carefully annotating spatial relationships between false positive objects and valid object pairs within 12,000 images. We further develop a relationship classification framework that categorizes spatial and non-spatial connections between valid object pairs and unexpected objects. We evaluate our model's performance on the WebVRD dataset, showing that ignoring spatial cues leads to poor results, and we showcase WebVRD-Loc's utility by integrating it into the training of visual relationship models, demonstrating that these unexpected objects are highly informative and valuable data sources.

The evolution of galaxies is significantly influenced by their structural components, yet little is understood about how different structural elements interact and transform. This study focuses on a galaxy group at a distance of 300 million light years, consisting of a primary galaxy with extensive starless disks and two smaller companion galaxies with recently formed populations. By analyzing the primary galaxy in detail, we discover a small, dormant bulge situated at the center of the galaxy, surrounded by an asymmetric distribution of stellar remnants. Spectral analysis reveals that this dormant bulge and a nearby patch of inactive star formation near the galaxy's boundary are composed of high-density material. Simulations suggest that tidal forces have caused material to accumulate on one side of the galaxy, resulting in the formation of a large starburst region and a small, dormant bulge through the migration of stars towards the galaxy's center. As a consequence, the primary galaxy's future development may see the dissolution of its temporary birthing area and gradual movement of its birthing material to the galaxy's core. In contrast, the companion galaxies in this galaxy group have undergone tidal interactions that have suppressed star formation and suppressed quasar activity in their former starburst regions and themselves.

On November 7, 2004, a significant solar flare of class X7.1 was detected at the leading edge of a coronal hole.  Despite the high-speed solar wind that followed and created prolonged, high-energy particle acceleration, neutron decay particles (NDPs) were not observed at Lagrange point (L1).  Analysis of data from the Gamma Ray Spectrometer (GRS) on the CGRO satellite revealed two distinct events of NDPs at different points along the orbit.  These NDP events are attributed to electron interactions in the Earth's atmosphere, which occurred roughly 20 to 40 minutes before each satellite passed through the plane of the Sun.  As a result of this enormous event, extensive electron fields were produced that lasted for more than a day and affected both sides of the magnetosphere.

This study analyzed the orbital evolution of 1,048 exoplanets with radius greater than one Earth unit. By examining 79 instances where significant orbital decay occurred within less than 500 million years after the star formed, we found strong evidence that these events were caused by interactions with the star rather than gravitational forces in the star's disk. A comparison with simulations of planetary disks further supports this assertion. However, this observed angular momentum migration mirrors a previously hypothesized process of partial magnetic braking saturation, suggesting an alternative explanation that involves significant levels of saturation in stars as early as when the planets were formed.

The rapid spread of false news across various media platforms poses a significant challenge in our society. To address this issue, numerous news false information detection methods have been developed and studied. A recent study reveals that a large language model's training leads to an emergent tendency to generate misinformation, making it crucial to examine whether such models are susceptible to false news statistics. Consequently, the researchers constructed the Emergent False News Detection (EFND) task, utilizing emerging network architectures and traditional feedforward neural networks (FFNN) for comparison. The EFND dataset was further refined to incorporate social media content, resulting in the Emefent False News Detection with Multimodal Data (EFND-M) dataset. However, this news false information at emergent stage becomes a challenging task due to the non-linear nature of neural network activations. To tackle this difficulty, the study proposes the use of a meta neural process network (MNPN) for emergent false news detection, demonstrating superior results compared to other baselines in both synthetic and real-world settings. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits interpretability, enabling the explanation of its predictions.

This study examines a cyclic transport equation, which represents a model for certain types of flow in complex, varying environments. The equation lacks a cyclic symmetry, and our research delves into its initial value problem under particular conditions where the equation's coefficients remain bounded and do not change abruptly. Under specific circumstances, and given certain constraints, we discover that the solution to this equation remains smooth over time. However, in general, we demonstrate how small alterations in the conditions of the system can lead to outcomes that diverge significantly in both position and time.

Recent advances in radio frequency system design have been driven by the development of constant envelope filterless approaches. These methods have explored combinatorial elements such as sequences, spreading codes, and filters along with associated performance metrics like autocorrelation and phase and amplitude properties. In the raceway model scenario, where filtering performance is critical, polyphase Golay complementary matrices (PGCMs) have been found to play a key role due to their unique property of having an almost vanishing autocorrelation sum. Although the foundational properties of PGCMs were established over seven decades ago, the underlying structure of "raceway-like" systems has not been extensively studied up to this point. Over the past decade, quadratic phase code (QPC) filters have become prevalent in this application, and it was recently shown that PGCMs are essential for creating single-sided constant envelope QPC. In this research, we investigate the structural properties of PGCMs in detail and present several new construction methods that include combinations of existing constructions that had not previously been possible, thus expanding the available pool of practical "raceway-like" system designs.

Swapping the quantum states of identical particles is an anatomically and mathematically unique process that can be explored using valley interference in semiconductors with two distinct valley bands. This process is typically explored in silicon, and although it is often theoretically examined with $s$-wave $F$-center silicon defects, we demonstrate valley interference and spin swapping with gate-controlled 2D atomic-scale silicon quantum dots. Due to their small tunneling current, these defects are difficult to detect, but quantum dots' electrical and magnetic properties can be easily measured, allowing for straightforward swapping networks to be created. Due to their linear arrangement, these networks are ideal for exploring valley interference and for studying the impact of particle anicity and valley coherence in greater detail.

Graph neural networks have gained prominence in analyzing and predicting the behavior of complex systems, particularly in predicting time-varying properties such as link formations and attribute changes. However, this approach primarily focuses on predicting specific graph dynamics and may not capture the broader system's behavior. To address this limitation, we investigate a fundamental framework for representing complex systems that include a graph and associated time-series data, including external variables that can influence the system, internal states that evolve over time and may be hidden, and interconnections between the graph and the time-series data. We then develop a graph neural network framework to infer the underlying dynamics of this framework, which can be applied to predict specific graph dynamics and overall system behavior. Our proposed method is evaluated using synthetic data and real-world data from the COVID-19 outbreak, showing its predictive capabilities and generalizability across different scenarios.

In recent years, significant interest has been drawn from topological combinatorics and homotopy theory to combinatorial structures, leading to the emergence of a new field of research. This drive originates from a desire to apply fundamental principles from these fields to a particular problem of partition counting, whose origins are rooted in the analysis of real fields, tropical varieties, and moduli spaces. As a consequence of this interest, several novel concepts, tools, and theories have been developed, including the formation of the homotopy categories of stacked graphs and the associated homotopy invariants of polytopes and their subdivisions.

Virtual injury testing involves subjecting an accident victim to repeated
impacts to gather comprehensive data without harming the patient. To make this
possible, synthetic datasets with altered impact frequencies must be produced
with statistical credibility. In this study, a novel method for generating
synthetic injuries with different severity levels is proposed. A novel network
is proposed building on the ad-vaese architecture via probabilistic graph
dependencies. This network is capable of preserving the structural properties
of injury data while generating synthetic data with modified levels of
irreversibility and rotational instability. A reduced time-to-computation
is achieved through network optimization. A synthetic dataset 17 times larger
is produced using this network in less time-to-computation than alternative
methods.

A significant improvement to the GP-2 PostProcessing language compiler was made by us, reducing its bytecode size by half and increasing its speed by 1.5 to 2 times. Our optimizations involve converting the interpreter's function call instructions into direct function executions, and implementing a more efficient byte code parser using look-ahead capabilities. These changes were developed with the intention of creating a compiler that minimizes the need for further optimizations to GP-2, potentially unnecessary given GP's versatile nature.

Representing text, images, and other data types in a consistent manner is
becoming increasingly relevant for cross-domain tasks. Various approaches for
extracting features based on deep learning have been developed, yet they lack
a single, cohesive framework. Our new approach, the Unified Matrix Based Feature
Extraction (UMBE) system, begins with a pure linear transformation, then moves
to a neural network-based method called the Neural Network Based Unified
Representation (NBURe), and finally incorporates contrastive learning in three
components: data preprocessing, loss computation, and the resulting unified
representation. We've specifically adapted the contrastive learning process for
text-based input in the NBURe system. Our proposal has two key contributions:
first, a completely consistent approach to representing multiple data types, and
second, integrating contrastive learning into the NBURe system's framework. In
practice, we've implemented the NBURe system using the Contrastive FreeAviton
representation, and our results show that this approach leads to significant
improvements in performance compared to other unified models when tackling
cross-domain classification problems.

A permutation group Q is termed "star normal" if it possesses a core that is isolated and its corresponding quotient is classified as a twisted wreath structure. In the context of mathematics, significant efforts have been made to identify collections of groups with specific properties that have isolated cores. A critical subfield, rational number theory, relies on collections of groups with properties that are termed "normal" and "star normal" to idempotent lifted twisted wreath (ITTW) congruences. Although certain collections of groups have been defined and utilized effectively, the development of broader and more diverse collections of groups that are "star normal" remains an intriguing research topic. A distinctive collection of groups that are "star normal" and of the ITTW was recently defined and utilized to idempotent lifted ITTW (ITTW) congrences with increased lower bounds. The collection in question is of infinite size and the individual groups within the collection are characterized by parameters that are prime numbers and integers that satisfy specific modular conditions. As the moduli of these conditions are relatively prime and the collection of integers that satisfy the conditions is both infinite and uniformly distributed across infinite collections of integers that are themselves products of the moduli.

Working with high-dimensional categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling is increasingly common, yet it presents unique challenges due to the infinite parameter space associated with categorical variables. To address this difficulty, regression models with an aim to induce sparsity have been developed, including the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) and Group LASSO. Although effective for numerical predictor variables, their applicability to categorical predictors is limited. In order to achieve interpretation and variable selection with sparse models for high-dimensional categorical data, our proposed "enhanced group LASSO" extends the group LASSO framework by incorporating both dummy variables for reference levels and effect coding for non-reference levels.
