This proposed method is successfully integrated into the R package eglasso, featuring an interface for intuitive model fitting and visualization. Empirical evidence from simulation studies and real-world data analysis demonstrates the superior performance of the "enhanced group LASSO" in terms of model prediction and variable selection performance.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance in various NLP tasks, but their lack of access to absolute time and domain-specific information due to their structured nature presents challenges. To address this, modern techniques such as neural search and deep representations have been utilized to integrate knowledge from vast knowledge bases. However, these approaches require significant computational resources and are impractical for real-time applications on personal devices. Our goal is to develop a cutting-edge method for fulling embedding external knowledge into large language models' parameters through simple, real-world data formats like tables and diagrams, as seen in the new technique called as Structured Knowledge Injection (SKILL). By leveraging advanced gradient-based techniques, our method seamlessly incorporates these visual and tabular knowledge sources, enabling more precise language generation. Our results show that this new injection framework leads to substantial performance gains across a range of benchmarks, as well as in simple practical applications.

When presenting vector maps to the public, map lines are often depicted with line joins to make them more visually appealing. Despite their simplicity in implementation, these line joins can lead to visual artifacts known as aliasing when a 3D scene is viewed from certain angles. This issue is particularly pronounced when map layers are superimposed on other 3D objects. To address this problem, an effective approach called Spatial Anti-Aliasing (SAAA) has been proposed. SAAA achieves this by strategically cropping and adjusting the geometry of line joins based on their visible area, resulting in a consistent color brightness across varying viewing angles. When applied to 3D visualizations of vector maps, SAAA demonstrates superior effectiveness compared to other anti-aliasing methods.

To enhance single-channel audio, ensuring sufficient information is conveyed, full signal context comprehension is crucial. Existing dual-path neural network approaches, with their parallel short-term and long-term feature extraction paths, effectively convey information and deliver high performance. However, these methods rely heavily on neural components, lacking interpretability and efficiency. Natural short-term and long-term context representations can instead be achieved via dual-frequency band analysis, efficiently implemented using filter banks, and offering better information preservation, access, and access efficiency. This study presents a Dual-Path Neural Network, where the natural context representation is based on filter banks, eliminating the need for neural components in the dual-path structure. It develops a simplified, efficient model based on this concept for end-to-end speech enhancement, combining filter banks with recurrent neural networks. This approach not only explains the dual-path concept but also provides a suitable natural context representation that enhances performance.

System(s) of convection equations widely applied in meteorology and oceanography demand numerical resolution of sharp interfaces and reduced computational complexity for multi-fluid modelling. By developing a novel approach utilizing flux vector splitting and contact-preserving numerical schemes, interface preservation can be achieved in numerical simulations. Prior to implementing such models in full-scale simulations, researchers propose performing multi-fluid simulations of basic convection phenomena, with the aim of understanding the complete system's capabilities in replicating the relevant atmospheric or oceanic processes under varying thermal conditions. Specifically, our proposed approach involves using a single-column model to simulate the Rayleigh-Benard problem, which yields results comparable to established results previously obtained using single-fluid models.

We investigate the dynamics of $N$ independent Jaynes-Cummings systems in sequence, where each system has its own independent initial conditions. Our goal is to study the emergence of a total entanglement among all $N$ atoms under certain conditions. By and large, if the initial fields are the same in each JC system, we found that a genuine $N$-partite entanglement of the atoms emerges as a result of their interactions with the independent JC systems. However, if the initial fields are correlated, a significantly longer duration of the atoms' sincere entanglement can be achieved. Moreover, we found that a part of the initial entanglement of the atoms can be transferred to the fields' part without deterioration of the future sincere entanglement duration. Finally, we found that a longer sincere entanglement duration can be obtained via shorter JC interaction times.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards various subjects.
For this purpose, we devise an LSTM-based method for classifying Twitter sentiments,
which accurately captures the emotional content of public posts.
For training, we utilize the Twitter Sentiment Dataset consisting of 1.6 million entries
sourced from UCD Mallowsify, and split it into training and testing subsets of 1.1 million
and 500k entries respectively.
Our model's performance is also compared to previous works using publicly available
Twitter sentiment datasets, and it demonstrates a 70.8% F1 score, a 73.1% accuracy, a
74.6% precision, and a 69.4% recall.

The occurrence of the shade paradox during greybody factor calculations indicates a violation of the first law of black hole thermodynamics. In this study, we re-evaluate the shade problem within the context of Riemann-Cartan spacetime by incorporating the spin-connection contribution to photon geodesics in charged AdS black holes without assuming a small charge-to-mass ratio. Our gravitoelectromagnetic approach yields an exact, integral-based energy spectrum that can be numerically assessed, allowing us to assess the influence of charge, mass, and anti-de Sitter radius on the shade problem. Our findings reveal the existence of a shade problem in adiabatic photon processes and propose that the photon charge induces a new form of black hole cooling analogous to the Peltier effect, which generates heat flow from cold to hot regions, causing shade to expand beneath the horizon and contract outside, leading to our second major conclusion: the photon Peltier effect governing adiabatic charged black hole processes and resolving the shade problem as a legitimate component of black hole thermodynamics by classifying the heat flow associated with photon greybody factor processes and integrating it into the first law of black hole thermodynamics.

Reconstructing a quantum state from Tomographic data is known as Quantum Tomography. 
We distinguish two types of quantum state reconstructions: direct reconstruction of the original quantum state, and another where the goal is to recreate a maximally classical state through a specific transformation process. 
Direct state reconstruction is accomplished via a "Tomogram-to-State" map, 
while achieving classical state reconstruction requires a distinct "Tomogram-to-Classical" map, 
resulting in a new phenomenon called "onset of classical tomographic synchrony". 
Onset of classical tomographic synchrony signifies that, given specific tomographic data, 
the original state and a classical state become indistinguishable. 
Two phenomena can cause departures from a flawless, one-to-one correspondence between the original state and a classical state represented by its phase-space distribution, 
namely, loss of coherence and entanglement. 
Using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) and W states as examples, we examine the onset of classical tomographic synchrony, 
as well as the onset of full-scale quantum entanglement synchrony and first-order quantum entanglement synchrony. 
Our analysis demonstrates that all three onsets share common features, 
thereby providing a general approach to studying the onset of synchrony in various quantum states within MW representation.

With the rise of immersive 360-degree video experiences, personalized
recommendations are becoming increasingly valuable. To achieve this, perspective
prediction from subtitles is pivotal, as it reflects the behavior of guided viewers.
However, there is little research focusing on this aspect in relation to
immersive videos. In this study, we develop a perspective prediction framework
for 360-degree virtual tourism videos, considering the unique characteristic of
viewers' perspectives converging on the same point in 2D projection space. To so, we
propose a subtitle-aware perspective prediction model (SPPM) that integrates
subtitle information to predict the bending direction within projection space. To
validate our hypothesis and model, we conduct subjective and objective
experiments, achieving significant improvements in objective results. Ultimately,
this finding serves as a crucial guideline for future work in immersive behavior
analysis.

Utilizing the tensor network approach, we investigated the conditions under which a given ensemble of thermal states or a specific initial state's thermal time evolution can be precisely represented. By leveraging the thermo-field dynamics formalism, we established that a lattice system's thermal state can effectively be represented as a long tree structure within a high-dimensional Hilbert space. We identify a straightforward criterion ensuring that tensor network operations on this tree structure preserve the fidelity of the state. Similarly, we found that tensor network representations of lattice system thermal states vary significantly based on the spectrum of the system's Hamiltonian. Moreover, our findings indicate that a long tree structure of dimension D/L in the system's Hilbert space results in thermal correlation decays that decay exponentially with a power law exponent of -2.

In this work, a scale-based decoupling theorem for bounded random variables holds true. Given a collection of centered random variables, $X_i$, with variances restricted to a maximum value of $\sigma^2$, defined within disjoint index sets $I$, the sum's variance is significantly greater than the sum of the individual variances by a factor of at least $K$. A decoupling result then shows that the number of variables, $n$, can be separated into two index sets, such that the sum's variance is comparable to the square of the sum of the individual standard deviations. A this decoupling technique is applied to obtain a new proof of a long-standing conjecture regarding the various formulations of the KLS conjecture, as well as a new proof of a lower bound for the conductance of Markov chains, derived from random walk dynamics.

The contribution of infrared renormalons to the nucleon color dipole gluon distribution's virtual contribution, denated as $F_g(x,Q^2)$, will be examined within the framework of QCD for the region of the $x$-Bjorken translation zero. A specific approach will be demonstrated to incorporate non-perturbative effects arising from infrared renormalons into the TMD gluon PDF, $\mathcal {E}_g(x,Q^2)$, at both the T-odd and T-even limits of the TMD PDF under certain conditions. Bessel function expansions, much like non-gaussian and gaussian TMD models, will be used as points of comparison. Based on global $\vec {x}$-SATSRAKT data fitting, predictions for the single gluon TMD PDF saturation function will be made and compared to the color area law prediction, as well as color glass condensate predictions for $x_g\approx Q_s$.

Using two-dimensional dielectric lattice structures combined with Bragg mirrors, we are able to create a novel type of lattice that allows for the transmission of light in a specific direction through a cleaved edge. This achievement overcomes the limitations of conventional lattice structures, where photons are trapped due to their high effective index, and it allows for both vertical and horizontal light transmission without cladding. By utilizing high-index silicon lattice structures in the infrared spectrum, we can enable transmission of light in perpendicular directions while maintaining confinement in other angles. By altering the geometry or using materials with different refractive indices, we can also adapt this surface lattice to other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Decision trees are widely used in various fields due to their effectiveness and ease of interpretation. However, traditional methods for optimizing decision tree structures are computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages a decision model trained via gradient boosting as a black box, enabling the extraction of patterns from training data to guide the construction of decision tree structures in a zero-shot knowledge transfer framework. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that this approach produces rules with higher accuracy than those obtained from traditional methods, and also leads to more efficient and equally valid transformations of the decision tree structure.

We have analyzed $3.0 \times 10^6$ $B^0_s$ decays that happen at a specific energy level to study rare processes. By measuring two key indicators, we calculated the relative likelihood of two types of $B^0_s$ decays in relation to $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^-$ events. We also considered theoretical predictions from different models to better understand these decays. We have established proof for two previously unknown $B^0_s$ decays, namely $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ with a relative likelihood of $146$ events per $10^6$ $B^0_s$ decays and $\bar{C}_{0+}(\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S)/(\bar{D}^0 K^-) = 0.40$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*+} K^0_S$ with a combined relative likelihood of $5.8$ per $10^6$ $B^0_s$ decays and a corresponding $\bar{0+}(\bar{D}^{*+} K^0_S)/(\bar{D}^0 K^-) = 0.04$.

Given the set of join irreducible elements of a lattice of submodules of a module M with no repeated composition factors in its structure, along with a function that defines the order relation between submodules, we can construct a lattice of submodules of M, under specific conditions where each composition factor appears exactly once. This construction method is illustrated using examples, including subspaces within a vector space, subgroups of an abelian group, and the Harder-Narasimhan lattice of subbundles within a vector bundle.

Reinforcement learning agents can significantly accelerate their task mastery by copying the actions of human demonstrators. To further exploit this benefit, we investigate a novel Co-Imitation Scenarios, in which the target system being observed for copied behavior is actually the one performing the task on its own, without the need for actual expert demonstrations. We establish coherent theoretical boundaries for this situation and outline key considerations and practical strategies for successfully executing Co-Imitation across a wide range of applications.

This paper fills a gap by establishing a metric for PAC codes, in response to the lack of a metric definition for these codes until now. We begin by reviewing key codemetrics including Hamming distance and K\"aehler metric before presenting a new metric based on the Golomb-Veerhuizen weight. The main objective of the paper is to provide a detailed algorithm for computing the distance between two PAC codes, along with an analysis of its efficiency.

Neural machine translation (NMT) produces translations through beam search, which aims to maximize the probability of a translation based on individual words. However, maximizing the probability of a translation often does not correspond to the probability of each word in the sequence, as suggested by prior research. Reinforcement learning (RL) was proposed to address this issue, treating the NMT model as an agent that makes decisions at each step of generating a translation. While effective, this approach requires a large amount of data and is inefficient due to the model's inability to generalize well beyond the training set. In contrast, our approach trains the NMT model with RL using an action space consisting of entire candidate beams rather than individual actions. This reduces the number of states to three: the current beam being on, a neighboring beam being on, or the target being in a neighboring beam. A neural structure was designed to learn the relationship between the NMT model and the action space, allowing for efficient training with minimal labels. Our approach significantly improves translation accuracy on the IWSLT'14 German to English dataset, as evidenced by our results.

To better picture non-equilibrium steady states resulting from periodic processes, an experiment with a single qubit has been used as a model system. Both the experiment and a corresponding simulation show that under certain circumstances, a periodically driven system reaches a non-equilibrium steady condition, where the outcomes of repeated measurements converge to a cycle that is independent of time. This finding expands on the concept of a "ratchet effect" previously demonstrated with a slow periodic process, demonstrating that it is also applicable to rapidly oscillating conditions.

A bi-holomorphic vector field, denoted as $X$, is found in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, where $n$ represents the dimension of an $n$-dimensional submanifold $\Sigma$. The submanifold $\Sigma$ is characterized by a specific property where the divergence of a certain combination of its geometric components remains constant, represented by the equation $\frac{1}{2} \left( \left( \Delta b + 2Kb \right) \right) \delta = \delta$. The recurrent structure vector field was initially proposed by researchers who focused on hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature, and it was later broadened to include various other geometric configurations by different scholars.

A rational function id(ID) equals ID for input ID if and only for ID belonging to a specific subset of 2_N, named id-IDifiable sets, this holds true when ID represents the formal language associated with a given class of automata or algebraic structures. This concept is equivalent to membership recognition problems. We identify id-IDifiable sets for finite automata, pushdown automata, and regular rational series, demonstrating that they are all the same class of sets, namely regular id-Dentifier sets. This finding contrasts with a earlier result showing that regular functions lack capacity to characterize subsets of power set of N. We also establish that subsets defined by regular id-Dentifiers form a frame.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented database that implements version
control-based transaction coherence, which allows it to schedule transactions freely.
Although this design provides great performance, it's crucial to confirm that
flagitious transaction scheduling actually schedules transactions in a coherent
way according to database protocols. Our work presents a consistent triad of
techniques to guarantee transaction coherence scheduling throughout the
system. Firstly, we analyze the transaction coherence protocol of MongoDB's
architecture in detail. Secondly, we propose a high-level, schedule verification
method that utilizes proof carriers to schedule transaction coherence protocol
validation. The schedule verification approach is realized as a plugin for the
actual database. Moreover, we develop a transaction coherence testing framework
to automatically generate robust test cases for the ongoing and future
development of the database. Our schedule verification tool and framework have
been made available to the public on GitHub.

In the context of graph theory, we define a new function $e$ that maps colored graphs to polynomials in variables that represent the counts of 2-edge-disjoint subgraphs belonging to different connectivity types. We demonstrate this function on proper colorings, showing that it corresponds to the well-known chromatic symmetric functions. Furthermore, we discover that two specific combinatorial objects, inverse Kostka triangles and inverse Kostka squares, can be extracted from this function. This combinatorial interpretation of $e$-positivity provides an foundation for a potential generalization of $s$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric functions.

Research on simplified binary networks that represent real-world phenomena has largely ignored hidden structural patterns, specifically triangle-based connections, in favor of simpler pairwise connections. This study examined a model of spin reversal dynamics in a (L, T)2c complex network, accounting for both pairwise and triangle-based connections, and observed a set of unique and concealed dynamical behaviors. The model, which displays both hysteresis and temporal oscillations, is highly influenced by the strength of connection forces and the proportion of triangle-based connections in the network. Notably, the model exhibits route multistability, where competing stability regions coexist, and has the potential to offer a novel, more concealed framework for understanding real-world interactions and dynamics involving both pairwise and triangle-based connections.

A knowledge of the interplanetary environment's physical characteristics is essential for comprehending how it affects outer space and celestial bodies in the inner solar system. The sun continuously releases charged particles into the inner solar system, also known as solar wind, whose speed, direction, and composition vary significantly. These fluctuations influence the distribution of particles in the inner solar system, influencing the movement and behavior of spacecraft, as well as the position and behavior of natural objects. The Inner Solar System Particle Environment (ISPI) project at Los Alamos National Laboratory is focused on understanding the sources, processes, and consequences of the interplanetary environment's variability. To achieve this, the project emphasizes the use of the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) to gather first-hand data from close proximity to the sun, complementing existing knowledge from previous missions. The PSP will make its first approach to the sun on December 5th, 2024, at a distance of 28 solar radii, and the Solar Breeze Energy Flux (SBEF) instrument package is designed to provide the first detailed observations of the interplanetary environment at this close range. The SBEF package will then support the broader goals of the PSP and the interplanetary environment research community.

A task with a significant societal impact, speech-emotion identification, is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data that reflects a wide range of emotions and the risk of inaccurate annotations due to the ambiguous and relative nature of theemotions themselves. These issues are compounded by the possibility that trainedemotions models may perform poorly when applied to new domains due to data distribution shifts. In contrast, low-cost utterance text transcription, along with readily available open-source datasets, present a valuable auxiliary source for enhancing and adapting low-resource speech-emotion identification models. In this study, we introduce a novel deep reinforcement learning-based framework that utilizes utterance text as an intermediate supervision signal, and carefully control the extent of knowledge transfer to prevent negative transfer. The resulting domain-adapted baseline and enhanced multi-hop baseline demonstrate superior performance on multiple datasets across several domain adaptation scenarios, outperforming the traditional baseline and even achieving high precision in addressing the range-emission challenge by potentially distorting the relationship betweenemotions and extending the low-resource scale ofemotions to the high-resource scale of text.

Researchers studying an expanding universe have recently discovered a way to model the early stages of the intergalactic medium's partially ionized state. By creating a three-dimensional simulation of a uniformly expanding universe with a spherical void at an extremely small comoving scale, they found a highly compact, shock-driven phase within the void during its rapid initial expansion. This study analytically examines a simple, compressive shock phase that occurs inside an adiabatically expanding spherical void in the universe. The conditions required for this intense shock to exist have been defined, and the characteristics of this unique shock phase have been examined in detail.

This study aims to characterize the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate in two dimensions.
Using $3.0$ inverse femtobarns of $\sqrt{s}=3$ TeV proton–charm production, we identified this rare decay process.
By applying an ensemble of $B_s^0$ and $D_s^{*-}$ production models along with systematic variations to account for uncertainty, we determined the parameters of a Chebyshev polynomial that describes the differential decay rate in two dimensions.
The resulting parameters are $c_0=0.69\pm 0.04$, $c_1=0.68\pm 0.13$, $c_2=-0.38\pm 0.10$, $c_{12}=0.38\pm 0.16$, $c_0(m_{\mu\nu})$ and $c_1(m_{\mu\nu})$ which vary with the $D_s^{*-}$ mass.

A recent paper provides an analysis of necessary conditions for a Schrödinger operator with constant mass to be free from monodromy, focusing on the case where the mass is not equal to 1/2 and showing its connection to orthogonal polynomials of Hermite type defined by entire functions. We offer examples of such polynomials, including generalized and non-generalized versions, as well as those corresponding to the Askey scheme. A specific set of conditions for the absence of monodromy is derived, along with its interpretation through the lens of Isomonodromic tau functions. An initial characterization of the set of potential functions that result in monodromy-free operators is also obtained, which, in the case of a mass of 1/2, aligns with findings from previous research.

A persistent issue in signal analysis that involves discrete events, such as identifying events in noisy data where individual events overlap and obscure one another, was examined using a simple experimental setup involving an adhesive tape being peeled from a flat surface at a constant speed. By analyzing the acoustic emissions produced during this process, researchers were able to identify the source of each sound event. They found that each event consists of a sequence of discrete "jumps" or "rips" of varying sizes that occur too quickly to hear individually but can be detected using microphones. It was also discovered that the number of jumps in each event follows a power-law distribution with a slope of 2, and that the average number of jumps in each event conforms to an exponential distribution. These observations were used to develop a theoretical model that can replicate the statistical characteristics of the acoustic signals. This model can help explain phenomena like event masking and may have wider applications to other "crackling" behaviors observed in condensed matter physics.

Recently, a new classification of higher-order derivative terms was proposed that circumvents tachyonic instabilities and ghostly states, when extending general relativity. A non-abelian ether-like term was shown to have valuable applications following this proposal. It was demonstrated during this lecture how the non-abelian ether-like term arises from non-abelian vector fields or gauge fields in both special and general relativity in finite temperature settings. Furthermore, it was explained how the non-abelian ether-like term leads to thermal phase transitions in special and general relativity settings.

This study introduces a new approach to hedging options by creating a dynamic delta-hedging strategy that accounts for the liquidation of hedging assets. This is relevant for institutions that option positions to evaluate the risk of options and over-the-counter derivatives. As a result, side constraints emerge when deciding how to hedge by purchasing or selling hedging assets. The possible outcomes are to buy or sell the hedging asset, or neither, depending on the current option position and the desired delta. The current desired delta is influenced by the cost of liquidating the hedging asset. The study derives the equation for the margin side constraint and uses it to examine the behavior of the current desired delta. The results indicate that the strategy is nonlinear and occasionally counterintuitive.

A dynamic, stochastic intergenerational mobility model shows that opportunity distribution significantly influences an individual's social class trajectory over time. The research reveals that even modest variations in opportunity distribution can lead to social class transitions, whereas extreme inequality in opportunity distribution results in poor current status predicting future success, akin to legacy effects seen in standard intergenerational mobility models. A collection of games was developed to simulate opportunity distribution, and one game in particular, featuring a public good, was used in experiments with 40 participants for 20 rounds each. Findings suggest that high-opportunity environments tend to promote equality, while high-opportunity-deficient environments lead to inequality, even among rational agents. Opportunity-deficient environments were found to have a stronger impact than high-opportunity environments. The research also discovered that the distribution of opportunities drives intergenerational persistence through legacy effects, rather than by influencing initial human capital.

Scan brightness diagrams effectively depict the relationship between an antenna's aperture distribution and its far-field radiation characteristics. 
These diagrams provide actionable information on beam properties such as side lobe levels, null depths, and crop efficiency levels. 
For point sources, the radius of brightness scan directly corresponds to the maximum dimension of the antenna's aperture. 
When applied to extended objects, such as beams with specific dimensions along two axes, scan brightness diagrams show the absolute side lobe levels in relation to the central lobe's peak. 
However, when a part of the antenna fills its entire aperture, the diagram's scale results in exaggerated, unusable values for absolute beam properties. 
To address this limitation, a revised scale is proposed that re-normalizes the scan plane, offering usable and directly interpretable values for predicting beam properties for any given antenna. 
This revised scale can be easily implemented in beam tuning processes to achieve desired characteristics.

This paper presents a optimization algorithm resistant to malicious influence, 
aiming to achieve the same outcome as classical gradient descent methods but with 
distributed computation and quantized data transmission. The proposed technique 
achieves this with enhanced security and efficiency, requiring significantly fewer 
bits to transmit than a previous solution. Specifically, the method uses 2n + 1 
bits to transmit to the leader, compared to N log N to N^2 bits in existing protocols. 
The paper proves convergence of the optimized algorithm under both synchronous 
and asynchronous settings, providing a comprehensive analysis of its performance 
even in the presence of malicious influence.

We developed a cosmic microwave background (CMB) instrumental filtering simulation tool, in the s4cmb package, to replicate real experimental conditions. Our simulation tool is rooted in the exacting physics and mathematical principles that underpin real experiments, to the extent possible, to accurately mirror the data an actual experiment would produce. We believe incorporating this level of fidelity is crucial to effectively prepare researchers working with upcoming CMB experiments such as the Simons Observatory and CMB-S4. To demonstrate the utility of our tool, we applied it to two real upcoming experiments and were able to reproduce their specific instrumental filtering effects, in collaboration with the experiment data teams. These effects are in addition to the well-known source of instrumentation, namely the non-ideal behavior of detectors. We specifically simulated this effect using existing models of the time-varying beam filters and frequency-dependent detectors.

In the task of arranging words, pre-trained language models like BERT excel due to their strong representation capabilities, yet their impact is still unclear. BART, known for its generation capabilities and KLD divergence-based evaluation, serves as an effective platform to investigate the role of representation in a generation task. Our research reveals that using a frozen BART model in the arrangement dataset leads to similar performance to that of simple baseline methods, highlighting its limited efficacy in this context. Freezing other components of BART during training results in performance levels comparable to those achieved when all parameters are trained. Our findings also indicate that the model's generation capability is the primary factor in solving the word arrangement problem, with the cross-likelihood metric showing a strong correlation to problem complexity. This research underscores the need for alternative evaluation metrics that better reflect the problems' inherent difficulty.

The rapid dissemination of videos and news via social media underscores the pressing need for an efficient deepfake detection method. Deepfake detection models have been significantly transformed by neural network architectures, yet they often lack interpretability and generalizability due to their complex "black box" nature and overfitting problems. This research proposes a novel neural network structure called the Mean Descriptor Network (MDN) and a novel framework called the MD-CSDNetwork that leverages conditional generative adversarial training. The MDN extracts generalized features from input videos, while the MD-CSDNetwork utilizes a novel cross-stitched design and dual data augmentation techniques to enhance performance across multiple related video adversarial tasks. The adversarial components of this framework enable it to generate hard samples for training, thus improving its generalizability. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of the proposed framework, highlighting its technical nuances and benefits in the context of deepfake detection.

In 1930, Menger presented a series of articles on the foundational concepts of metric geometry, introducing the concept of angle metric and outlining two problems concerning the characterization of Euclidean metric spaces. However, the subsequent developments in this field were built upon by Kantor, and other researchers who did not interpret the angle spaces in the same way Menger did. According to the original definition, the characterisation of the dimension one should be based on the additivity of angles rather than the power of the resulting angle, which this paper aims to clarify by providing the necessary adjustments and a proper mathematical framework. With these corrections, two theoreme can recover the dimension concept as used in the geometry of Euclidean space.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n$ over the rational numbers and Minkowski's successive minima $\lambda_i$ for an ordered convex convex set $\Omega$. When the average values of $\lambda_1$ for all primitive directions within a height limit are examined, we find that for a specific number field with $n=13$, $\lambda_1$ typically scales as $c^n t^{(2/
 R)n+o(n)}$, where $t$ represents the height, and the constants $c$ and $
 R$ are derived from the geometry of numbers and the theory of Euclidean spaces. However, if we examine $\lambda_1$ for all possible primitive directions within a certain distance from the origin, we find that $\lambda_1$ usually scales as $t^{(2/
 R)+o(1)}$. These findings build on previous research by various mathematicians who explored the distribution of residues and the geometry of numbers.

The paper presents the cluster character function for a specific class of quantum groups, denoted as $Q_{cluster}(\vartheta_t)$. A key property of this function is that it preserves the localizability of polynomial algebras under a certain quantum parameter $t$. The study establishes a connection between these polynomial algebras and a specialized variant known as the cluster-PO pre-atomic limit at $t=0$. The work extends a earlier discovery made by Leclerc and Zelevinsky, initially for the $t=1$ case, and generalizes the results obtained by Leclerc through additional research.

Forsage, which unwound as one of the largest pyramid schemes of 2020, attracted over 1.6 million participants worldwide and generated approximately $280 million before it was shut down. This study provides an examination of the Pyramid Selling Investment (PSI) business model that Forsage implemented, and traces the code of its accompanying cryptocurrency protocol. We discover that the smart contract for this protocol was programmed with features to support the fraudulent selling of packages and rebate mechanisms inherent to the PSI business model, and found that the contract's state, in particular the status of these packages and associated rebate accounts, was frequently modified through numerous undeclared backdoor functions.

A catalog of potential globular clusters has been assembled within the VVV South Galactic Bulge survey data, covering a four square degree area. A subset of 19 clusters, which were absent in previous studies, whose locations precluded identification by the Palomar survey, were examined. The color evolution of main sequence stars for each object was analyzed to establish their variable star periods and ultimately to confirm their authenticity as globular clusters. The data indicates that VVV has an capacity to discover GCs in far-reaching areas, which can vary based on the brightness of the main sequence turn off. VVV has a capacity to study GCs near the Galactic center, which was previously considered impossible.

In order to capture and evaluate the limitations of holographic quantum error correcting codes, we have developed the hyper-hereditary multi-scale eigenstate renormalization group algorithm, which we've termed HERM or, simply, Mermaid. This simulation incorporates spatial and basis space deformations that occur during each virtual tensor movement within the Mermaid architecture. We have implemented a highly efficient, linear N-body time-stepping solver, utilizing an optimized multigrid method to accelerate dynamics simulations. This approach allows us to bypass typical time-stepping limitations and instead simulate complex, $1/f$ noise-like dynamics on large systems, even when working with long-range interactions and boundary conditions on gravitational timescales, all while applying a relevant dual-gravity model of tensor movement dynamics encoded within the Mermaid architecture. Notably, our studies have yielded a universal, yet unexplained, constant that arises from a balance between the competing interaction orders.

Deep-learning methods have been widely applied in process discovery, prediction, and mining, yet achieving significant performance often requires substantial computational resources from complex neural architectures, a contrast to simpler and computationally efficient models like random forests. This study aims to compare several deep-learning approaches including BPTT, LSTMs, and RNNs, against traditional algorithms such as logistic regression and random forests for the purpose of discovering, predicting, and understanding business processes, a task critical to optimizing business performance. Our study uses real-world data from a payment processing company, and our key findings reveal that RNNs yield superior results for process discovery and understanding, whereas RSTMs and random forests perform equally well for process prediction, a result a downstream classifier leverages for predicting subsequent process tasks, based on accuracy, F1-score, execution time, and model size metrics.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, denoted as $S^{\sigma,\rho}$, in both their standard and modulation-theoretic variants. The spaces $S^{\sigma,\rho}$ consist of functions that are sufficiently smooth and whose Fourier transforms are limited to specific polynomial growth regions, with particular focus on demonstrating that these spaces are not merely trivial (functions equal to zero) when the sum of $1/(2\sigma)$ and $1/(2\rho)$ is less than or equal to one, and $1/2+\epsilon$, and similarly for the modified conditions with $2\sigma'$ and $2\sigma_{p}^{\prime}$. Additionally, we establish a criterion that ensures these spaces are not trivial, and as a consequence, we characterize the Toeplitz operators in the standard setting, where they preserve the $Q_{0} = S^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon,\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon}$ space, and we confirm that no non-zero Toeplitz symbol can preserve this space in the standard scenario.

A massive stellar flare occurred on April 12, 1985, on AD Leo, a nearby star, and was given the designation SS Aur.  This event held a significance of approximately $3.0$ and lasted for about two hours, featuring an X-ray brightness that exceeded its pre-flare levels by four to five orders of magnitude in the 0.3 to 2.0 keV range.  The flare showed characteristics both typical and unusual, with prolonged durations in the near-ultraviolet and soft X-ray spectrum but shorter than expected in the far-ultraviolet range.  The near-ultraviolet features showed brightness increases of a factor of a hundred to a thousand compared to usual levels.  To understand the energy release during this flare, we developed a simulation using a standard four-state radiation hydrodynamics flare model, which, however, fell short in explaining the event's duration and intensity, particularly the lasting effects on H$\alpha$ and the lack of rapid fading of the Fe XXV line.  The flare may have resulted from the interaction between a stellar comet and a plasma stream, which could have also explain the unusual properties of another massive flare on Barnard's Star.

Neural network models based on convolution and attention mechanisms have achieved significant success in processing structured data through the use of superpixels and graph nodes. However, these methods introduce parameters that vary between datasets, making them transformationally unique and difficult to generalize. In this work, we present a approach called transformation-unique smoothing for point cloud models. By applying a simple smoothing operation to the intermediate outputs of a PointNet, we reduce the dimensionality of the parameter space to a constant value, regardless of the input dimension. This allows us to implicitly learn the graph structure and demonstrate that our approach outperforms comparable methods on various tasks, including binary classification and segmentation.

This study develops a rigorous mathematical approach, based on Jost functions and the Random Phase Approximation, to characterize the structure and energy characteristics of atomic nuclei like $^{16}$O in detail. By applying this method, researchers can examine the characteristics of atomic nuclei, including their energy levels, wave functions, and density distributions. In order to further examine the energy levels of atomic nuclei, the characteristics of jost phases are broken down into their constituent parts. A fundamental aspect of this study is the investigation of the ground and excited states of $^{16}$O, including one particular state with specific energy and angular momentum properties. Additionally, this study explores various structural features of a specific excited state of $^{16}$O, including its energy, wave function, and density distribution.

Clustering techniques are widely utilized in various domains such as machine learning, pattern recognition, and statistical analysis. In particular, they play a key role in organizing large datasets into meaningful groups. Unlike supervised methods, the development of unsupervised clustering algorithms is more challenging due to the absence of pre-defined group labels. Although some successful unsupervised algorithms exist, they often lack a clear interpretation or practical significance. Moreover, traditional evaluation metrics for statistical clustering fail to capture useful impacts of data partitions. This work presents a novel framework for developing and evaluating unsupervised dynamical system clustering techniques based on three interconnected components: feature selection, ensemble construction, and useful-partitioning optimization. An application of this framework results in a new unsupervised dynamical system clustering method called DBI-VAE, based on two key innovations: the use of dynamical invariants as local coordinates for clustering and the incorporation of domain knowledge and potential applications in optimizing partitions through tree-based methods. The effectiveness of DBI-VAE is validated through numerical simulations and real-world data analysis, demonstrating its high performance and versatility in analyzing complex dynamical systems.

Deep text generation techniques relying on large neural networks face significant hurdles due to the complex, unstructured nature of language data and the problem's severe sequence-dependent shifting patterns. In contrast, simpler models utilizing sparse representations have achieved remarkable success in various language generation tasks. This study introduces two novel generative network architectures based on a sparse generative adversarial network framework, addressing two major challenges in text generation: non-stationarity and data sparsity. We develop the Attention-Sparse GAN and the Character-Sparse GAN, both incorporating external language knowledge and avoiding the need for extensive neural models. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of these approaches, with the Attention-Sparse GAN generating 1.5 times more diverse and grammatically correct sentences and the Character-Sparse GAN producing 20-character longer solutions with a 0.5 F-score improvement over current state-of-the-art methods.

The concept of interstellar panspermia was first proposed by A.G. Crookes in 1879, suggesting that life could be transferred between galaxies or star systems within the same galaxy. For life to survive the high-speed travel through interstellar space, it must be contained within resilient structures like meteorites, asteroids, or comets. While the extreme conditions of the interstellar medium (ISM) pose a significant challenge to the viability of interstellar panspermia, studies indicate that a small fraction of comets may retain sufficient integrity to facilitate the transfer of life within the Milky Way. Based on these findings, future missions like the Breakthrough Starshot may have a non-negligible probability of discovering evidence of interstellar panspermia by analyzing the debris from nearby comets.

Animal population studies often benefit from incorporating individual behavior, 
specifically resource choice, into capture-recapture models that use spatial 
data and telemetry. By integrating telemetry information with resource choice 
observations, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of key capture probabilities 
and develop more accurate models of species' capture processes. However, capture-
recapture models using spatial data typically rely on random capture processes, 
which may not reflect the structured capture processes exhibited by many animals. 
This discrepancy can result in biased estimates of capture probabilities and 
underestimated models of the species' capture process if telemetry data related to 
species behavior is ignored. By utilizing telemetry data to model capture processes, 
capture-recapture models can be significantly improved and better reflect the 
actual behavior of the species being studied.

The dynamics of interconnected systems have been modeled using a multilayer network without a concept of 'within-layer' interactions. Our work presents a modified model where each individual layer now has its own internal interactions, and links between layers can either make or break. We then analyze the model's stage-dependent behavior, both with and not with time-vanishing interlayer connections, and find that it can either extend or compress the range of possible multistability states. We further investigate how the model's interlayer connections' arrangement influences the evaluation of the complex multilayer system's effective connections in the search for the volterra response. Our findings are shown visually through water wave-like phase patterns across different configurations.

Given the symmetric properties of both strain and stress tensors, there are six independent components in total when analyzing the constitutive operator in solid mechanics. This research delves into the mathematical characteristics of the linear and nonlinear elastic operators, specifically the Cauchy stress operator $\Sigma$, by seeking its minimal parameterization. We examine both the linear case, where $\Sigma$ is viewed as a sixth-order tensor, and a linearization at an arbitrary prestrain state, as well as the strictly nonlinear case. In each scenario, we use the Specht algebra to characterize the smallest set of independent material parameters required to fully define the elastic response, effectively capturing the essential "stiffness" of a wide range of materials in both linear and nonlinear contexts.

The integration of formal methods and automated testing has yielded geometric testing systems that utilize test cases as variables to generate concrete and retest cases, facilitating bug discovery and verification.

Consider two finite groups G and K, with G being a normal subgroup of the direct product GK. Let Ω represent the set of nonzero vectors in a specific vector space formed by elements of the group algebra FG. We are interested in vectors that maintain a consistent distance from one another. It has been found that if the number of components of the highest-dimensional irreducible representation of k is more than one, then the vector space formed by the highest-dimensional irreducible representation of K includes a circle of 162 distinct directions. If the number of components of the highest-dimensional irreducible representation of K is three, then the same vector space includes at least 26 distinct directions.

Determining the underlying graph structure is a fundamental task in network estimation problems. Typically, algorithms for this purpose aim to achieve $\Theta(d)$ scale by utilizing $O(\poly(d,\log n))$ samples, with a few exceptions that produce even more accurate results. However, in real-world scenarios where the network is noisy or compromised by malicious actors, our focus shifts to an innovative scale estimation problem under Byzantine faults. We introduce a robust scale estimation estimator $\hat{d}$, which guarantees with high probability, either the true degree lies within $[\frac{\hat{d}}{C_1},\hat{d}C_1]$ or the degree of a malicious node lies within $[\frac{\hat{d}}{C_2},\hat{d}C_2}$, where $C_1$ and $C_2$ are constants. To accomplish this, we first devise an initial algorithm in a faultless setting that consumes $O(d^3\log^3 n)$ samples, and then, to enhance efficiency, we present a concentrated version of this estimator in $O(d^2\log^2 n)$ time, which consumes $O(d^3\log^3 n)$ samples, thereby fulfilling our primary objective.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric method for estimating short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating their parameters.
The proposed estimator, based on actual traffic data, can accurately predict
queue lengths regardless of whether they follow a random process.
A theoretical analysis reveals the estimator's reliability in various
scenarios, providing replacements for previously known parametric methods.
The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation experiments,
along with the development of a link between the nonparametric approach and
traditional kernel density estimation.

In simulations of numerical relativity, representing gravitational waves and matter at the boundaries of a spatial space is a common approach. However, this method involves solving a set of non-linear integral equations to determine a set of initial data. These equations are difficult to solve due to their non-uniqueness and the difficulty in determining a unique solution. Various methods have been developed to find an approximate solution, but they suffer from issues such as non-uniqueness and difficulty in convergence. In the EDDINGSTONE code, we implemented a new algorithm to find a solution, which involves using a set of compact variables and a novel formulation of the equation in terms of these variables. This method has been shown to converge in a wide range of scenarios, including those with rotating black holes and neutron stars. Our method is particularly well-suited for use with high-resolution spectral methods, which are employed in the EDDINGSTONE code to solve the initial data equations.

We observed the unusual Nernst effect in Mn3NiN epitaxial thin films, which show remarkable magneto-transport properties similar to bulk wurtzite MnNiN.  At temperatures below 100 K, we found very large, oscillating Nernst signals that respond differently to clockwise and counterclockwise magnetic fields, with particularly high efficiency in regions of antiferromagnetic domain wall.  These findings provide strong evidence for the existence of such domain walls and indicate that the Neel vector is likely oriented parallel to the film surface.  We observed lower nernst signal strength in cubic MnNiN phases compared to the wurtzite phase, suggesting that this phase has better potential for practical applications involving the Nernst effect.

The rapid advancement of machine learning and AI is set to significantly enhance the efficiency and capabilities of modern user facilities, such as synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers. By integrating these technologies, user facilities can provide a more efficient and tailored experience for the vast number of scientists utilizing them. Specifically, machine learning can enable the simultaneous operation of multiple experiments, streamline complex setups, and personalize the user experience at the user interface. These benefits can be witnessed by the vast user community, numbering over 100,000 professionals and students from diverse fields including chemistry, physics, and materials science. To illustrate the potential applications, this talk will draw examples from the Canadian Light Source in Saskatchewan.

Consider the following non-autonomous obstacle problem:
$$
\begin{cases}
\Omega_1: & u(x) \geq \psi(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}^n, \\
\Omega_2: & \mathcal{Q}(t)u(t,x) = -\partial_t u(t,x) - \Delta \big(u(t,x)^{\gamma}\big) = 0,
\end{cases}
$$
where the matrix-valued function $\mathcal{Q}(t)$ is uniformly elliptic for all $t > 0$, and $\gamma$ is a constant greater than one. Given an initial condition $u(0,x) = u_0(x)$ and an obstacle function $\psi(x)$ that is non-negative, we are interested in understanding the regularity properties of the solution $u$. Specifically, we aim to prove that the gradient of the solution, $\nabla u$, is locally essentially bounded in time and space. Moreover, if the initial condition, the matrix-valued function $\mathcal{Q}$, and the obstacle function satisfy certain boundedness conditions, then we can establish that $\nabla u$ is also continuous. These regularity properties of the solution have significant implications for any obstacle that satisfies weakly local solvability conditions.

We develop in Kummer theory a clear introductory explanation through global unramified Galois extensions, accompanied by useful applications. In addition to applying it to an GL_2 case, we obtain certain new results. Through an non-trivial clear relation in Kummer theory we can characterize the set of weight dividing the conductor f, clear means unsing any local or modular form theory. Through an non-trivial clear relation with the reduction map we can determine the image as an open subset of (residue field)^f.

The concept of isoperimetric residue posits that, in a setting where the scale of mean curvature $\sigma$ and the ambient space's geometry coexist harmoniously, a surface can approximate an ideal shape to minimize area while adhering to specific curvature and geometric constraints, with any shortfall accounted for by a small, localized discrepancy relative to the scale of the surrounding space. In a recent breakthrough, a conjecture stating that, under identical conditions, the scale of the surface and the ambient space's curvature align smoothly, with any deviation represented by an inherently scale-appropriate surface with minimal area and no excessive curvature. Building on this foundation, we introduce a novel approach to achieving optimal surfaces that minimize area while adhering to specific curvature and geometric constraints within their respective environments.

Structural health monitoring and damage control in composite structures depend on accurately detecting and locating structural defects. Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) has emerged as a promising technique in this field due to its rapid, non-invasive nature and capability to generate resistance maps of structures. This study integrates EIT and a genetic algorithm to pinpoint the physical location and severity of damage in composite structures, with results showing precise detection and quantification of artificial and impact-induced damage, with errors less than 5 percent and 10 percent respectively.

Eluding firewalls is an incredibly complex task for firefly swarms, an observation
that led us to an intriguing hypothesis: firefly swarms possess a heightened
intelligence compared to individual fireflies. This gave rise to our "Less Clever
Elements, the More Intelligent Whole" theory. It prompted our inquiry into the nature
of swarm intelligence, specifically how a large group of simple beings can exhibit
a collective behavior that surpasses the capabilities of any single one. To address
this question, we developed a purposeful swarm of micro air vehicles (MAVs), which
allowed us to investigate the concept of emergent properties in a controlled
environment. Our research was guided by three primary research questions, which
focused on whether a swarm can display a novel, unexpected property that is not
found in its constituent parts, an emergently property that is not found in the
components of a purposeful individual, an intelligent property that is not found
in the components of a purposeful individual. Our study explored the concept of
purposeful swarm intelligence and provided answers to these research questions, as
well as a valuable lesson about the significance of defining purpose in the
development of advanced systems.

This work explores the fundamentals of tensor calculus in a generic coordinate system, focusing on key geometric concepts such as vectors, base vectors, and metric tensors. It outlines the computation of Christoffel symbols and the associated tensor, as well as the distinction between covariant and absolute derivatives of a tensor. It also highlights essential properties of these derivatives, including their utilization in defining the curvature tensor.

The discovery of $B_c^-$, a beauty-celearton, in Fermilab's data has been serendipitously favorable, given $B_c^-$'s surprisingly wide natural resonance. This natural longevity could be attributed to a narrow phase space for hadronic decay or perhaps a smaller decay width. To further explore such long-lived vector beauty-cealearton states, theories such as Axion-like particles and Majorons were considered. Though these theories typically produce abundant $B_c^-$ mesons through hadronic decay, their natural longevity is not particularly high. However, there is a chance to naturally explain the observed natural resonance by replacing a specific decay constant in their Lagrangians with a particular combination of $B_c^-$ meson masses and mixing angles.

The generators of global symmetries in Toda conformal field theories exhibit universal properties that are independent of the specific group and apply to all levels c. By examining the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT, we provide explicit examples of how the energy-momentum tensor and primary fields share the same status as "semi-primary" representations, closely related through a process analogous to a modified form of BPS saturation. This process involves the application of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Ward identities, signaling an intrinsic $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ duality within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT. Furthermore, we identify the precise conditions under which the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda CFT can be regarded as a consistent limit of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ theory, revealing two distinct ways in which it arises as an effective low-energy approximation of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT.

If two Cayley graphs, derived from the same Coxeter system, share the same underlying undirected structure, then they are equivalent. This equivalence implies that the Coxley graphs of a given Coxeter system are automatically unique in a causal sense. Further research reveals that all groups resulting from Coxeter transformations are bi-automatic.

Recent advances in non-invasive brain-computer interfaces have shown significant potential for applications like movement rehabilitation and adaptive training programs. However, to achieve this, it is crucial to accurately identify the underlying patterns in brain activity that correspond to different modes of walking. Researchers have developed a novel approach using state-space models and electrocorticogram data to automatically discover these patterns. By employing this method, they were able to identify both the phases of a gait cycle and the associated step rates from a participant's walking recordings. In addition to this, they were able to replicate previously published findings and successfully apply their method to a new dataset, replicating key results and obtaining both phase and step rate estimates for each step taken by the participant.

Connectivity estimation is a crucial task in analyzing complex systems, yet it becomes a challenging task in dynamic settings due to the intricate relationship between elapased time and network parameters. In the context of data-driven scenarios with limited access to underlying system information, our goal is to develop an efficient method for efficiently estimating dynamic networks, specifically focusing on a common case where the network changes gradually over time. Our approach, known as DeeCE (Deep DyNaMic EfFiCient connectiEstation), utilizes selective reuse of recent memory buffers to manage the interplay between network parameters and time, leveraging neural operators to generalize background knowledge and achieve adaptive and sample-efficient learning. Our research presents theoretical guarantees regarding data efficiency, and our initial experimental results showcase the DeeCE framework's versatility in tackling various time-varying network problems, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and demonstrating a promising direction for efficient neural approaches to dynamic network estimation.

Predicting movement in living organisms is a fundamental challenge for both artificial intelligence and humans. Although we can easily differentiate moving entities from inanimate objects in simple scenarios, numerous factors, such as our own motion, the behavior of animals, and the movement of objects in the water or air, can confound water-based, land-based, and aerial transportation respectively. Recently, a new dataset, termed as BioMoving, has been introduced to address the problem of biological motion detection in video footage. The BioMoving dataset contains 5,490 short video clips that depict biological motion and 10,000 background video segments lacking biological movement. Furthermore, bio-moving objects within the short video clips of BioMoving are labeled at the segment level to provide sequential information. Notably, BioMoving is the largest publicly available dataset for biological motion detection. It should be emphasized that detecting biological movement is not an easy task, thus it is suitable for both researcher exploring sequential learning and practitioners with real-world applications in mind.

Recently, non-equilibrium conditions have facilitated the creation of Anderson insulators with linear Hall conductance, resulting from localized defects. This innovation enables the realization of the integer quantum Hall effect through static, spatially localized defects. In this study, we demonstrate the Intergational Quantum Hall Effect using cold-atomic gases and a binary random disorder model, allowing for a detailed examination and theoretical understanding. Our numerical research reveals that localized Haldane models lead to distinct spatial regions of integer quantum hall states, which vary based on the strength of the disorder. Our study also explores the nature of this local disorder and its effect on transversal and longitudinal conductivities in a range of disorder strengths.

This research paper focuses on the fundamental concepts of cuts and morphisms within the context of category theory. It begins with Frenkel and Schreiber's formulation of 1-forms as categories, building upon earlier work, and discusses the Frenkel and Schreiber description of smooth manifolds as sheaves of categories. A key aspect of our discussion is a more in-depth exploration of these ideas.

The occurrence of at least one heavy at least 13 TeV on-shell Higgs boson is a key feature of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. The particle's properties, such as the mass, are complex and can be influenced by the decay of stop quarks. In certain parameter spaces, the on-shell Higgs mass becomes inaccessible, which significantly impacts the production of at least one 13 TeV Higgs at the Large Hadron Collider. To investigate this constraint, researchers utilized SOFTSUSY and SUSYHTQ to generate event simulations, using the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and SHiPaCo for further analysis. The outcomes of these studies were explored in an interactive 3D visualization tool, revealing that the at least 13 TeV on-shell Higgs exclusion primarily occurs when the muon parameter is at least 100 GeV and the on-shell squark mass is at least 200 GeV, regardless of the gluino mass. The results of this research indicate that approximately 90% of the allowed parameter space in this scenario leads to at least one heavy at least 13 TeV Higgs, detectable at an integrated luminosity of at least 3000 pb^-1.

This work formulates and analyzes the novel problem of learning in heterogeneous distributed contextual linear bandits, where each agent's learning context is fundamentally different from others. Specifically, the differences in settings are so distinct that standard aggregation techniques, such as those used in transfer learning, cannot be effectively applied. To address this challenge, we develop a decentralized learning algorithm that enables agents to learn independently, achieving a novel non-i.i.d. regret bound of O_d((p_0 + p_1 log T)^(1/2) + p_0 log T), where p_0 and p_1 represent the number of contextual features, and T represents the total number of iterations. This result demonstrates that the proposed method allows each agent to achieve a context-specific regret bound that is comparable to the optimal individual bound achievable in a fully observed, isolated setting. Furthermore, we provide a practical example showcasing the setting difference, and through simulations, we show the effectiveness of the designed algorithm.
